r: Brut is a local-first, bring-your-own-key node canvas for orchestrating generative-AI providers — Google Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, Kling, Veo, Seedance for generation; Magnific and Topaz for upscaling; OpenRouter, fal, Higgsfield and Replicate as aggregator routes when you'd rather hold one key than six. Your keys. Your machine. Zero markup. Brut never sits between you and the provider — every generation call goes straight from your computer to the provider, billed to your own account at their price. A working archviz graph: stills in, a contact sheet of viewpoints, a correction pass, a 4K upscale, every step on your own keys ## The idea in one breath Most AI tools are a website that holds your key, runs the model on their servers, and marks up the price. Brut inverts that: Bring your own key (BYOK). You paste your provider keys once; they live in your OS keychain and are used only for direct calls from your machine. Local-first. The app and a small engine run as two processes on your computer. Graphs, outputs and projects live on your disk (or your NAS). Nothing routes through a server anyone pays for. Zero markup, ever. Calls go from your machine to Google/OpenAI/Kling/etc. at their price. Brut is never in the call path. Never pay twice. Every node hashes its inputs — unchanged work is served from cache for free. Re-run a graph after a client note and only what actually changed costs money. If you work under NDA, this matters: your renders go only to the provider you pick, on your key — never to us.

Two processes, one machine: Brut app ──HTTP──▶ Brut engine ──HTTPS, your keys──▶ the providers the node canvas adapters + job queue (local) Gemini · OpenAI · … The app is the node canvas you work in. The engine is a small local server that holds your keys, talks to each provider, and writes outputs to your disk. When you launch Brut, the engine serves the app to your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8723/app/ — there is no hosted version, by design.

Images — text-to-image, image-to-image, inpainting, composition, and multi-shot exploration (a whole contact sheet of viewpoints from one scene, with a deck of surprise cards so the takes never repeat). Corrections — Annotate & Correct: draw arrows and notes on a render, attach a reference, and the model applies exactly those changes; Layers paints the original back wherever the model overreached — local and free. Compose by hand first — the Sketchpad: brush strokes and wired images as movable layers on one canvas, flattened locally into the image you generate from, plus the mask of what you drew. Free. Video — animate stills into clips with Kling, Veo or Seedance, with an itemized cost quote before a cent is spent. Whole films — the Cinema Sessions: a crew of AI agents (scenarist, art director, DoP, script supervisor) that plan a sequence from your stills, which you then shoot and cut locally with ffmpeg. Delivery resolution — upscale stills and clips to 4K/8K with Magnific or Topaz (or your own local Topaz Video AI, free). Ready-made workflows — a shipped bank of pre-wired chains for the recurring jobs (clay to photoreal, day to dusk, populate, weather, an editorial sheet, a hero still to a clip, and more): each drops as one card with knobs, on named models, from the home screen or the library. See Workflows. A studio companion — Marcel reads your canvas, narrates what happened, advises on models and looks, and can build graphs for you on request — on your own key, every call in the ledger.

Install & first run — get Brut running and sign in. Your first image — a three-node graph, start to finish. Nodes & graphs — how the canvas thinks. Marcel — the companion that lives beside the canvas.
Brut is a native Windows app: one installer, one window. No Python, no terminal, no browser tab.

Windows 10/11. A billing-enabled API key for at least one provider (see Providers). A free-tier key usually has zero image quota — a first-call 429 means billing isn't enabled, not rate-limiting. That's it — the installer brings everything else.

Download Brut-Setup.exe from getbrut.app/download — log in with the email address your beta approval was sent to (that address is your access; your approval email links straight there). The sign-in email carries a link (press Continue on the page it opens) and an 8-digit code you can type on the page instead, handy when your company's mail system opens links before you do. Windows SmartScreen will warn about an unrecognized app — expected: the beta build isn't code-signed yet. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer runs per-user — no admin prompt — shows the beta license, and adds Start-menu and desktop shortcuts. Launch Brut from either. The window appears in a couple of seconds; the engine starts (and stops) with it. A tray icon in the notification area shows the engine's status and offers the engine log and Quit.
Install the desktop app › Where things live

Your work — projects, outputs, library, account state — lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut, as plain files on your disk. Your keys live in the OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager), never in a file. The engine log is at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs\engine.log (previous launch kept as engine.log.1) — attach it when reporting a bug. Uninstalling never deletes %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut — your projects and keys survive uninstall and reinstall.

No auto-update in the beta: getbrut.app/download always serves the latest build — when we announce a new version, download it there and run it over the old version. Projects, keys and sign-in all carry over. Brut does check for you: at launch, while signed in, it compares your version with the latest installer and shows one line under the toolbar (Brut x.y.z is available, with a Download button) when you're behind. Up to date means nothing is shown.

Brut requires a free account (it's how we count seats during the beta — nothing about your prompts, images or keys is ever sent). On first launch you'll hit a sign-in screen: Continue with Google or GitHub, or Email — enter your address. The email carries a link (open it and Brut finishes signing you in) and an 8-digit code you can type into the same screen instead. Use the code when your company's mail system opens links before you do: it uses the one-time link up, the code still works. Sign-in is required, but it never bricks you: once you're in, a 30-day offline grace keeps you working through flights and outages, and if the sign-in server is ever unreachable a "continue for now" option appears. The engine holds your session; the browser keeps nothing. Right after your first sign-in, Brut shows the beta license once and asks you to accept it (again only if the license changes). Your seat is personal: please don't pass the installer around — someone else wants in? Ask them to register on getbrut.app.

Click the key icon on the left rail (or the setup wizard walks you through it on first run). For each provider, paste your key and Brut validates it on save. Keys are stored in your OS keychain — never in a graph, never sent anywhere but the provider. The setup wizard: paste a key, Validate, done. Keys go to the OS keychain, never to us ### Your first project On first launch the wizard also asks where your work lives: name your first project and choose its folder, a local folder or a share on your NAS. That step cannot be skipped — every graph, result and ledger row you make lands in a project, and the starter graph that follows lands in this one. Create more any time from File ▾ → New project…, and move a canvas between projects with File ▾ → Save project as… (see Projects & the ledger). You can also set keys via environment variables before launching the engine (GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, etc.) — handy for a shared workstation. See each provider's page for where to get a key and its billing quirks. The quickest start is Google Gemini — a gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image (Nano Banana 2 Lite) render is about $0.03.

Brut opens on a home screen, not a bare canvas: the place the day starts from. Continue — the big card is your live canvas: which graph, which project, when it was last saved, and its latest results as the cover (hover it to flip through the last five). Continue (or Esc) puts you back on it. Beside it, What's new lists Brut's development and the models that joined the catalog, newest first, each entry linking to its docs or changelog page (the list scrolls); when a newer installer exists, the first entry says so with a download link. Recent graphs — every saved graph across all your projects, newest first, each carrying its project as a colored badge. Two rows show at a time; the pager at the gallery's lower right (arrows around a "1 / 3" counter) turns the pages. The cover is the graph's own most recent result; hover it and it flips through the last five results downstream (the dots let you pick one), so you see what that graph made, not one frame. A • next to a name means the canvas holds changes not yet saved to it (the card then shows the canvas' own results). Click a card and Brut switches project if needed and opens the graph; the usual "unsaved work" guard still asks. The select narrows to one project, the search box to a name. Workflows — New graph first (it asks for a name and saves the starter graph under it, so you never land on unsaved work), then the workflows that ship with Brut and the ones you saved, as cards with their picture. A template starts a new graph; a composite drops onto your canvas as one card. Hover a cover that holds a pair and it shows what went in, then what came out. The chips filter by category, the label you give an item when you save it; two rows show, Show more adds two. The last tile, Open the library, opens the full gallery. Brut opens on the home screen: Continue where you left off, recent graphs from every project, templates to start from The **house icon** on the left rail (just above Settings) and **File ▾ → Home** bring the screen back any time. The checkbox at its bottom, **Show this screen at launch**, turns the landing off; the house icon still works.

The window has two homes for controls. The top bar is workspace chrome: the File ▾ menu, the project and graph selectors, the spend readout, ▶ Run, your account, and the engine status dot. ▶ Run is a two-step button: it first reveals, replaying every cached, pinned and free step for $0 and marking the nodes whose inputs changed with a needs a run badge (they keep their last result on the face); if anything would bill, one dialog itemizes it with the estimate, and you choose Generate or Keep cached only. The ▶ on a node runs that node and its upstream straight away, as before. The left rail is your tools: add a node, undo/redo, tidy, the Library, Marcel, the home screen, keys, feedback, and the theme toggle. Hover any rail icon for an instant tooltip with its name, its keyboard shortcut, and one line on what it does — and the » pin at the rail's bottom expands it to show labels next to every icon (on by default; collapse it once the icons feel familiar). The rail on the left holds every tool and panel; the top bar keeps only the workspace chrome The rail's **+** opens the **node browser**: every node grouped by category — Inputs, Text, Images, Video, Cinema team, Utilities — plus your saved Library composites. Hovering a row shows what the node does, what flows in and out of it, and whether it **costs money** ($), is **free**, or is free with a paid option inside (**free · $**: the Sketchpad draws and flattens for free, only its generation layers bill a model). Click a row to place it at the canvas center, or drag it to drop it exactly where you want. (Pressing `Tab` over the canvas still opens the quick palette at your cursor — the fast path once you know the names.)

Right after the setup wizard, Brut walks you through the interface once — a short spotlight tour of the canvas, the node families, projects, running & caching, the spend ledger, Marcel, and where your keys live. Skip it any time with Esc, and relaunch it whenever you like from File ▾ → Functionality tour.

The Marcel button on the left rail (the pulse icon) opens the studio timeline — a chronological feed of what the engine is doing: planner reasoning, shot lists, runs, results, and errors. It's the home of Marcel, Brut's built-in companion, who'll chat and advise here in a coming update; for now it's your project's running diary. The timeline is saved with the project, so reopening it (even after a restart, or on another machine via a NAS share) shows the continuous history. A Raw events / Chat only toggle in its header hides the engine chatter when you just want the highlights.
Found a bug? Tell us from inside the app

The green speech-bubble button on the left rail opens Send feedback — a bug, an idea, anything. Reports go straight to the team, tied to your account email so we can reply. Diagnostics (app/engine version, OS, recent error messages) are opt-in, and the modal shows the exact payload before you send — never your graphs, images, prompts or keys. Details in Privacy. When you quit the desktop app after a session that ran something, Brut asks for a one-line note on how it went ("Before you go"). It's the same feedback form with a session summary on top; Quit without sending is always one click, and nothing is sent unless you press Send & quit.

If the engine dies mid-session, the desktop app tells you — a dialog with the last lines of engine output and a button to the full log — instead of a frozen window. If the app shows an "engine offline" banner, relaunch Brut. And if launch fails with "Port 8723 is taken", some other program on your machine is using Brut's port — close it and relaunch.
Let's make one image end to end. This takes about a minute and costs roughly $0.03 on Gemini's cheapest image model.
The fastest path: the starter graph

The setup wizard offers a starter graph on its last step, right after it has you create your first project — a ready-wired Prompt → Refine → Text→Image → Preview chain on gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image (Nano Banana 2 Lite). Click Add starter graph, then hit ▶ Run in the toolbar. Done. (Re-open the wizard any time from File ▾ → Setup wizard….) Add the starter graph, press Run, watch the image land with its cost on the badge If you'd rather build it by hand, here's the same thing in three nodes.

Add a Prompt node. Press Tab over the canvas (or + Node) and pick Prompt. Type a description: A sunlit modern villa at golden hour, floor-to-ceiling glass, a calm reflecting pool, photographic Add a Text→Image node. Drag from the Prompt node's output onto empty canvas — the add menu opens filtered to compatible nodes; pick Text → Image. It wires up automatically. In the node, choose provider Gemini and model Nano Banana 2 Lite (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image). Add a Preview node the same way, wired from the Text→Image output. Run. Click ▶ Run (or the ▶ on the Text→Image node to run just it). ▶ Run never generates blindly: it first replays everything that is already cached (free), then asks once, with the estimate, before anything is generated. On a fresh graph that is one dialog: Generate calls Gemini with your key, downloads the image to your project's outputs folder, and shows it inline. The node badge reports the cost. Drag from an output onto empty canvas: the menu opens filtered to what fits, and the pick arrives wired That's the whole loop: **prompt → generate → preview.**

The engine made one call to Gemini on your key and saved the result to outputs/ in your active project. The node cached the result against a hash of its inputs. Run again and it's free — nothing changed, so nothing is re-billed. Change the prompt and only that node re-pays. See Never pay twice. The generation was recorded in your project ledger — click the 🕘 on the node to see its history and re-pin any past result. The 🕘 on any paid node: every past result, and one click pins it back as the output, free ## Troubleshooting 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on the first call → your Gemini key isn't billing-enabled (the free tier has zero image quota). Enable billing in Google AI Studio. See Google Gemini. A ⚠ "Add your … key" button on the node → that provider isn't configured; click it to jump to the wizard. finishReason: OTHER (or IMAGE_OTHER) on an image edit → a silent content refusal, usually triggered by an input image (a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo) rather than the prompt. Remove or crop the offending image.
Refine your prompts with the Prompt Helper. Image generation — editing, inpainting, composing. Multi-Shot — a contact sheet of viewpoints from one scene.

Brut ships with a small bank of ready-made workflows: chains of nodes already wired, with their prompts and models set, for the jobs that come back every week. You find them in two places: the Workflows row of the home screen, and the Library gallery (the book icon on the left rail, or File ▾ → Browse library…), on the From Brut shelf. Every card on this page is generated from the same files the app ships, so what you read here is exactly what drops on your canvas.

A composite drops as one closed card with a few knobs on its face: a brief, a mode, a shot count, the model of a stage. Wire your image into its inlet, set the knobs, press Run. Open the card (⤢) when you want to see or edit the nodes inside. A template drops onto your canvas too, as a group of live nodes named after it. Nothing is hidden; edit anything. (Nothing on a card starts a new graph: that is the home's own New graph tile.) Every image stage is pinned to a named model at a named size, so a workflow gives the same kind of result on every seat. Video and upscale stages ship unset: the provider choice, and its price, are yours. The card tells you when a stage still needs a pick. Try with sample, on the workflows that ship with one, copies a sample picture into your project and drops the workflow already wired to it, with the shipped result on the card (captioned sample result) so you see what it does before paying for a run. Nothing runs until you press Run; a real run replaces the sample result. A card glows while a stage inside it renders, like any node, and its title bar carries 🕘 (every past take of a stage) and ↻ (a fresh take of a stage); a card with several stages asks which one. Cards whose result is a clip rest on the still they take and play the clip on hover. Once a card has a result, its Next chips offer the workflows that usually follow: one click drops the next card beside it, wired to the result. A dropped card is frozen at the version you dropped: it never changes under you. When Brut ships a newer version of that workflow, the card shows a small vN in the library chip; drop the workflow again to get the new recipe. Your own saved composites and templates sit on the Yours shelf, as the same kind of cards. The Never pay twice rule holds inside a workflow: a changed knob re-renders the stage it writes to, everything else stays cached.

Brut is a node canvas. You build a graph — nodes connected by wires — and run it. Nodes are shots and decisions, not samplers and latents: a node is "generate an image," "animate this clip," "plan the film," not a low-level knob.

Add a node — the + on the left rail opens the node browser: every node by category (in workflow order), with a hover card showing what it does, what flows in and out, and whether it costs money. Click places it at the canvas center; drag drops it where you let go. Or press Tab over the canvas for the quick palette at your cursor — type to filter, ↑/↓ + Enter to place. With nothing typed the list is alphabetical (so is the list a dragged wire offers); typing ranks the matches. Pan — middle-drag. Box-select — left-drag: anything the rectangle touches is selected, nodes and wires (a box drawn over a bundle of wires alone picks them up, wires light up as the box sweeps over them and when you hover them; Delete then removes everything selected). Zoom — scroll wheel, anywhere on the canvas, including over a board or contact sheet whose tiles all fit. Only a grid that actually overflows takes the wheel for itself, to scroll its tiles; text areas do the same. Left-drag selects, middle-drag pans, the wheel zooms, Tab opens the node menu at the cursor - **Wire** — drag from an output port to an input port. Drop a wire on empty canvas and the add menu opens, filtered to compatible nodes — pick one and it's placed *and* wired. Three gestures work on wires you already have, all explained under [Ports and wires](#ports-and-wires): **double-click a wire** to splice a node into it, **`Alt`-click a wire** to split it with a dot and send it to more nodes, **`Alt`-click a pin** to move all its wires to another pin. - **Wire style** — the three wire buttons on the left rail (curved, straight, stepped) set how every wire in the graph is drawn. One style per graph: it's saved in the graph file and `Ctrl+Z` undoes a switch. Old graphs open curved, exactly as before. - **Snap to grid** — the **magnet** on the left rail. On, a dragged node lands on the canvas dots (the dots *are* the grid, 24 units apart); off, nodes go exactly where you drop them. It's a preference of this computer, not of the graph, and it stays as you left it. Magnet off, a node stops between dots; magnet on, it lands on them and lines up with its neighbor - **Move children**: the toggle under the magnet. On, dragging a node drags everything upstream of it (its inputs, their inputs, through composite ports and reroute dots), the way a linked hierarchy follows its parent in a 3D package; off, a drag moves only what you hold. What a node feeds never rides along. Nodes already in your selection move once, never twice. A preference of this computer, like the magnet. - **Opening a graph fits it to the window**: from the home, the graph switcher or a file, the canvas lands zoomed on the whole graph, never on where the last viewport happened to be. Undo, autosave and Marcel's additions leave your view alone. Pull a wire off — an input pin holding one wire: press it and drag, and you pick that wire up instead of starting a new one. Drop it on another pin to move it there, on empty canvas to remove it (Ctrl+Z puts it back), on a pin that refuses it and it snaps back. A click without a drag changes nothing. Inlets holding several wires (a board's stills) keep the usual new-wire drag, and Alt on a pin is still the bulk rewire. Wire menu — right-click a wire: Color (Auto follows the node the wire leaves, None keeps it plain, or one of the six hues — applied to every selected wire when the clicked one is part of a selection), Add reroute here (the Alt-click split), Insert node… (the double-click splice), Delete wire. Node menu — right-click a node: Color, Run, Duplicate, Group, Collapse to composite, Delete. With several nodes selected, Duplicate and Delete act on all of them, and Group / Collapse light up. Text fields and image previews keep their own menus. Node color — pick one of six hues (the same ones group frames use) from the node menu. The whole node takes the color (body, outline and title — readable zoomed far out), and so does every wire leaving it — the fastest way to read a dense graph. Right-click one node of a selection and the color lands on all of them. Reroute dots pass the color along; a wire can also be given its own color from the wire menu; a hovered or selected wire still shows the accent. Run — ▶ Run executes the whole graph; the ▶ on a node runs just that node and everything it depends on. Copy, paste, duplicate — Ctrl+C copies the selected nodes, Ctrl+V pastes fresh copies, Ctrl+D duplicates in one step. Copies keep their incoming wires: a duplicated node arrives already fed by the same upstream nodes as the original (outgoing wires are not duplicated — that would double-feed whatever the original feeds). Ctrl+V pastes at your cursor — point where you want the copies and paste; a multi-node selection keeps its arrangement, and a copy pasted inside a group frame's area joins that group (exactly like dropping it there). Ctrl+D still lands the duplicate just beside the original. Paste an image — Ctrl+V with an image on the OS clipboard (Photoshop Ctrl+A+Ctrl+C, a render buffer's Copy button, a browser image) drops a ready-filled Image In node at your cursor. If you copied both, whichever you copied last wins the shortcut. Tidy — the grid button on the left rail auto-arranges the graph as a table that follows the wiring: columns are the pipeline stages, and every node joins the row of the node it is most specifically wired to, so a Prompt, the Multi-Shot it feeds and that Multi-Shot's Shot Board share one row with their tops aligned, even when one base image feeds every Multi-Shot (the shared base gets a row of its own). Independent chains stack top-down in the order they were and never interleave. A pool of siblings (several nodes with the same parents and the same children, like eight Image Inputs feeding one board) wraps into a compact grid, a 3×3 contact sheet rather than a tower. With two or more nodes selected, only those are tidied, in place: the block keeps the selection's top-left corner and nothing outside it moves (select a group frame to tidy its inside). It's one undo step — Ctrl+Z puts everything back. Node ids — every node's title bar shows its id in small type (multi_shot-21). That's the name Marcel and the ledger use when they refer to a node — click the id to copy it.

Every node exposes typed ports. Wires carry one of three things: images, text (prompts and plans), or video. Ports are labeled by role — a Compose node has scene and reference image inlets. Brut only lets you connect compatible types, and picks the right inlet automatically when you drag-to-connect. Some nodes expose per-tile output plugs — a Shot Board tile has its own handle so you can route one chosen shot downstream, a Clip Board tile has one per clip.
Ports and wires › Splice a node into a wire

Double-click a wire (or right-click it → Insert node…): the add menu opens, filtered to the nodes that fit between the two ends. Pick one and it lands on the wire, wired in and out — an Upscale between a generator and its Preview, a Conform in front of a board, without redrawing anything. Double-click a wire, pick a node: it lands on the wire, wired in and out ### Split a wire with a reroute dot Alt-click a wire and a small dot drops on it at that point: the wire now runs through the dot, and the dot is a branch point. Send the same output to more nodes — drag a new wire off the dot to any compatible input. Drop it on empty canvas and the add menu opens, filtered to what the wire carries; the node you pick arrives already wired. One output feeds as many nodes as you like, and you branch from where you are instead of going back to the source node. Route the wire around things — drag the dot (Substance style). Add more dots for more bends. Right-click a wire → Add reroute here does the same. A dot has one inlet and as many outlets as you drag off it, and it carries the color of its wire along. It's purely cosmetic: execution, caching and pins see straight through it, so nothing downstream re-runs or re-pays, and Marcel doesn't see it. Delete a dot and the wire heals: its input reconnects to every wire that left it, nothing is left dangling. Alt-click a wire: a dot drops on it; drag a new wire off the dot and the same output feeds a second node ### Move wires between pins (`Alt`-click a pin) To re-plumb a graph without redrawing it, Alt-click a pin. Every pin on the canvas starts pulsing: a rewire is armed on that pin (the Activity panel says so). Then click the destination pin (Alt no longer needed): Same kind (an output, then another output; or an input, then another input): every wire on the first pin moves to the second, and their other ends stay where they are. Five nodes fed by one Prompt? Alt-click its output, click the output of a new Prompt, and all five are fed by the new one. An input, then an output: whatever fed that input now comes from that output — "feed this from there instead". An output, then an input: the wires leaving that output are pulled onto that single input. Click the armed pin again, press Esc or click empty canvas to cancel. Two wires that would end up on the same two pins merge into one. The Activity panel logs what moved, and Ctrl+Z undoes it like any other edit. Alt-click a Prompt's output, click another Prompt's output: every wire moves across in one go ## The execution model When you run, Brut topologically sorts the graph and executes on a promise-graph scheduler: each node starts the moment its inputs are ready, so independent branches run concurrently. Two things make this cheap and fast: Input-hash caching — a node whose inputs haven't changed and that has a cached output is skipped, free. See Never pay twice. Handle-aware routing — inputs are grouped by role, so a node knows which images are the "scene" vs the "reference," and which tile's output a wire carries. Run: independent branches execute at the same time, unchanged nodes answer from cache instantly Runs can overlap if their scopes don't share a node. Paid work is guarded so nothing double-pays.

Family Nodes Inputs Prompt, Refine (Prompt Helper), Text→Text, Text Board, Image In Image generation Text→Image, Image→Image, Inpaint, Compose Exploration Multi-Shot, Shot Board, Reference Board Cinema team Director (plan + proof sheet), Storyboard Video Image→Video, Film Shots, Clip Board, Sequence Utility Conform, Preview Each family has its own page under Nodes in the sidebar. Sticky notes, emoji stamps, the pen and text labels aren't nodes — they're annotation tools in the rail's Organize section, also one right-click away via the ring menu (all documented on the utility page).

The canvas autosaves into the project itself (a .workspace.json beside the saved graphs, written moments after every change), and it remembers which named graph it is — relaunch the app in any mode, or reopen the project from another machine on a NAS share, and you land exactly where you left off, name in the selector and all. Named saves are still explicit (File ▾ → Save, Ctrl+S); a • next to the graph name means the canvas has changes not yet saved to it, and opening another graph over unsaved work asks first instead of silently replacing it. Undo/redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) covers structure and parameters — never generation results, which are the ledger's job, so undoing a param edit keeps your caches warm. Delete a node by mistake, Ctrl+Z brings it back with its results intact

A project is a first-class container: it owns its outputs, its saved graphs, and its ledger. Everything you make lives inside the active project on disk. Switch projects from the toolbar's project selector; the whole workspace swaps. Started building in the wrong project? File ▾ → Save project as… takes the current canvas into a brand-new project of its own — name it, pick its folder, and everything moves with it: every image and clip the canvas references moves into the new project's outputs/ (same subfolders). A file that another graph in the old project also uses stays there as a copy, so nothing else breaks; the ledger rows of the carried nodes move too, so 🕘 history and spend show up in the new project, and the files those past takes reference come along; if the canvas was a saved graph, its file moves with it and keeps its name; the graph is rewritten to the new locations and stays warm: unchanged nodes replay from cache on the next Run instead of re-paying. The graph file remembers which outputs folder it moved from (pathCompat), and every cache check tries that former location before declaring a node stale — a real edit still misses, as it should. The old project is left with a fresh canvas. Rows that clearly belong to another graph there (they are tagged with its name) stay put. The log line under the action says how many files and rows moved and how many stayed as shared copies. Wait for a running generation to finish first — the action refuses while a job is in flight. To find any result on disk, right-click its preview → Reveal in Explorer. Create a project (File ▾ → New project…) and choose where it lives — a local folder, or a share on your NAS. NAS-rooted projects store their data at any absolute path (a project.json marker inside makes it portable). A second seat can Open project… on the same folder and adopt it — that's how a studio shares live work. Default project keeps the legacy outputs/ location, so nothing you already made ever moves. File holds the actions; the two switchers beside it only switch, project and graph Projects can be **exported** whole (outputs + graphs + ledger) to an empty folder — the copy is itself openable — or packed into a single **[.brutpack](/docs/concepts/brutpack.html)** file.

Every terminal generation — success, failure, or cancel — is appended to the project's ledger (ledger/generations.jsonl). Each row carries the full request context: node id, provider, model, prompt, the output paths, and the cost estimate. Text and planning calls are ledgered too: Text → Text, Refine, the Multi-Shot planner and the cinema crew each write a planning-lane row with the provider-reported token counts, priced from the catalog's per-token rates (Marcel's own calls have their separate companion lane). No spend is invisible. The ledger powers two things: Per-node history & re-pin. Click the 🕘 on any generation node to see everything it ever produced, and pin a past result as the active output. See Never pay twice. Spend. The toolbar readout aggregates the ledger into a running total, broken down by provider — and clicking it opens the full ledger: per-lane totals (generations vs Marcel's own calls) and every row newest-first with its model, status, and estimated cost. Budgets. File ▾ → Project budget… sets a spend ceiling for the project. The readout shows $spent / $budget and tints as you approach it (amber past 80%, red past 100%), and every paid confirmation dialog adds an honest budget line near the cap. Budgets are soft by default — they inform, you still hold the OK. Tick hard cap and paid confirmations refuse instead until you raise or clear the budget. Comparisons use the ledger's estimates; leave the amount empty to remove the budget. Click the spend readout: the ledger panel, per provider and per node, with the budget cap on top Because the ledger is written at the moment a job *finalizes* (not when it's submitted), jobs that were reattached after an engine restart still price and record correctly — paid work is never lost.

Video jobs are asynchronous — you submit, then poll. Brut journals every async submission and reattaches in-flight jobs when the engine restarts, under the same job ids. If you kill the engine mid-render, the job recovers on the next launch — one ledger row, correct price. Unreadable journal entries are quarantined loudly rather than silently dropped.

<project>/ outputs/ generated images & video (+ .thumbs/ display copies) graphs/ your saved *.brut.json graphs ledger/ generations.jsonl + pending/ (async job journal) project.json the portability marker (for rooted/NAS projects) Keys are never here — they live in your OS keychain.

Every file Brut writes into outputs/ is named so the folder reads on its own, without opening anything: <project>_<graph>_<node>_<provider>_<model>_<date>_<job>.<ext> tournesol_facade-study_t2i-12_openai_GI25F_260923_a3f91c2e.png tournesol_facade-study_film-3-c02_kling_K30_260923_0c77e4b1.mp4 tournesol_facade-study_sb-2-kf-s3_gemini_NB2_260923_5d10aa07.png project and graph are the names you gave them, shortened to a slug (untitled while the canvas is not saved as a graph). node is the node's id with its kind abbreviated (t2i Text → Image, i2i Image → Image, i2v Image → Video, ms Multi-Shot, up Upscale Image, sb Storyboard, film Film Shots, dir Director …) and, for the nodes that make several files, which one: ms-4-s07 is Multi-Shot 4's shot 7, film-3-c02 is Film Shots 3's clip 2, sb-2-kf-s3 the keyframe of card s3 on Storyboard 2 (-end for a generated end frame), dir-1-proof a proof sheet. provider is who made it: the provider that actually served the call (a routed job names the aggregator, fal or openrouter), or the free local tool for its own results (conform, layers, sketch, sequence, tvai). model is the model's short code, in capitals so it stands out, for model tracking at a glance. A routed job still names the model you picked; the provider segment says who served it. Free tools have no model, so the segment is simply absent. It is what makes every name unique (two graphs called the same thing collide on nothing), and it is how a file finds its row: right-click any picture → Find in ledger shows the run that made it — model, node, graph, prompt, parameters, cost, date — and opens the node's 🕘 history on that row when the node is on the canvas. It works for files with the older random names too, as long as a ledger row lists them. Files you bring in (outputs/inputs/) keep your own filename: tournesol_facade-study_facade-photo_in_260923_ab12cd34.jpg (paste for a clipboard image; the key is a content hash, so the same picture dropped twice the same day is one file). Exports keep their readable stems in outputs/exports/. Files made before this convention keep their old names for good: a stored path is a reference, and renaming would orphan every cache and pin. Path length. A full name is 55 to 75 characters. Windows caps a whole path at 260 characters unless long paths are enabled, so a project rooted very deep on a server has less room for the name than for the folders. Brut never fails on that: when the full path would not fit, the name drops the project and graph segments, then the node, and keeps the traceable tail (date_job), which is shorter than the old random names ever were.
