Compose before you generate. The Sketchpad is a simple painter on a fixed canvas: brush strokes, wired images placed as movable layers, generation layers that render your marks in place, one stack. It flattens locally, for free, into the raster the generators consume. In the node browser it wears a free · $ chip: drawing, placing and flattening cost nothing, the generation layers are the paid part, and only when you ask for one. Typical use: block massing or a silhouette over a site photo, place an object where it should go, scribble the shape of a change, then wire the result into Image→Image, Compose or Inpaint and let the model render what you drew. One quick stroke on the lawn of the site photo, the spark, 'a group of people playing and listening to music': a generation layer renders them in place; the layer's mask painted white shows the whole group ## Ports images (in): any number of images. They do not flow through by themselves: they appear in the editor's tray, and you drop the ones you want in as layers. image (out): the flattened canvas as a PNG. (An earlier build also exposed a mask plug with the painted coverage; it is retired until a node can take a mask wire, and any wire saved from it is dropped when the graph opens.)

The first wired image sets the canvas size. With nothing wired, pick a preset on the node (1K or 2K in 1:1, 16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4). Once a sketch exists the size is locked; ✕ start over on the node clears the sketch and unlocks the choice. The canvas select (top of the right column) is what the flattened image shows wherever nothing covers it: white or black paper, or transparent for a PNG with alpha. With a wired photo as the bottom layer you never see it; erase a hole in that photo, or start from a blank canvas, and you do.

The tools sit in a rail on the left of the canvas, Photoshop-style; the bar above the canvas shows only the active tool's properties. Hover a tool for its shortcuts. The right column starts with the canvas select and the canvas size. Color works like Photoshop: a foreground / background pair in the properties bar (the brush paints the foreground; click the back square or press X to swap, D resets to black over white), an HSB panel at the top of the right column (the field is hue across and brightness down at the current saturation; H, S and B sliders with numbers), and a recent colors strip that fills with every color you paint or pick, kept per device. Brushes: six tips sit next to the color pair when the brush or eraser is active, each with a stroke preview. Hard round (the default, pressure drives the width), soft round, pencil (thin and grainy, a light touch stays faint), marker (a flat chisel that turns with the stroke: thin one way, wide the other, one width regardless of pressure), hard square and soft square. Picking a tip sets the softness slider and the two pressure boxes (size, opacity) to the tip's defaults; all three stay yours to override, so a soft round can drive opacity, or a pencil can keep one width. A mouse always paints at full pressure. The eraser uses the same tip. Your last pick is remembered on this device. Brush (B) and eraser (E) paint on paint layers. Size, softness and per-stroke opacity have sliders (while you drag one, the brush circle shows at the center of the canvas so you see the change), Alt + right-drag adjusts the brush like in Photoshop (horizontal = size, vertical = softness), with a Diameter / Hardness / Opacity readout beside the circles (solid = size, dashed = softness extent). With a mouse the cursor stays pinned; with a pen hold Alt, press the barrel button and drag (tip first then barrel, or barrel first, both work), the pen simply follows and the Windows press-and-hold ring is harmless, [ ] change the size, digit keys set opacity (5 = 50 %, 1 then 2 quickly = 12 %, 0 = 100 %). Pen pressure (Wacom & co) scales the stroke width; strokes are stamped, so the width follows the pressure smoothly through curves. After each stroke a small readout next to the pressure boxes says what arrived: pen · 78 % (pointer type and peak pressure) or mouse · no pressure. The second one means the tablet driver is sending mouse events, not pen events: enable Windows Ink for Brut in the tablet driver (Wacom: the app's Mapping tab) and pressure comes through. Shift+click draws a straight stroke from where the last stroke ended: click once for a dot, Shift+click elsewhere for the line. Eyedropper (I), or Alt held in any tool: press on the canvas to sample the composite, a swatch with the hex value rides the pointer, drag to hunt the exact pixel, release to pick it. Bucket fill (G): click a region to flood it with the current color at the stroke opacity. The tolerance slider widens what counts as the same color; sample all layers (default) reads the whole composite so you can fill inside the lines of a placed photo, unticked it reads the active layer alone. Transform (T, Ctrl+T, or V) shows handles on the selected layer: drag anywhere to move, drag a corner square to scale about the center (Shift+corner scales width and height independently), drag the stem handle above the top edge to rotate (Shift snaps to 15°). Works on paint layers too. Selections: the marquee (M) drags a rectangle, the ellipse (Shift+M cycles between the two) an ellipse, the lasso (L) a freehand shape. Shift at the start of a drag adds to the selection, Alt at the start subtracts, a plain drag replaces it, a plain click deselects. Pressed after the drag started, Shift constrains the marquee to a square or the ellipse to a circle and Alt grows the shape from the point you started at, like Photoshop. Ctrl+A selects everything, Ctrl+D nothing, Ctrl+Shift+I inverts. Ctrl+click a layer's thumbnail selects its painted pixels, like Photoshop (Ctrl+Shift+click adds them, Ctrl+Alt+click subtracts); Ctrl+click a mask chip selects the mask's white. Handy to recolor a shape: Ctrl+click the thumb, then Alt+Backspace. While a selection exists the brush, eraser and bucket only touch the inside. Ctrl+C copies the selected pixels of the active paint layer, Ctrl+X cuts them, Delete clears them, Ctrl+V pastes the copy as a new paint layer in place, with the Transform tool ready to move it. Selections live in the editor session only. Alt+Backspace fills with the foreground color, Ctrl+Backspace with the background color, like Photoshop: the active paint layer's pixels, or its mask when the mask chip is active (the color's grey level: white reveals, black hides). A selection confines the fill. One undo step. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo inside the editor (also the two arrows at the bottom of the rail): strokes, transforms, layer changes, background. The stack resets when you close the editor. Layers (right): the layer opacity slider at the top acts on the selected layer. Below it, the stack, top first, the only part of the column that scrolls. Eye toggles visibility, Alt+eye solos a layer (Alt+eye again restores what was shown), + (or Ctrl+Shift+N) adds an empty paint layer right above the active one (inside its group if it has one; on top when nothing is selected), ↑ ↓ reorder, 🗑 deletes (a group takes its children along). Drag a row to move it in the stack: the row lifts and a blue line shows where it will land; nothing moves until you release, and names never change. The 🗑 removes every selected layer. Double-click a name to rename it; right-click a row for a color label (Photoshop's eleven, shown as a colored edge, purely for organization) plus hide, rename and group. Layer masks, on paint layers, image layers and groups, exactly like Photoshop: the mask button in the tray (or the row menu) adds one, white = shows (Alt on the button adds a hide-all mask). The mask chip appears right of the layer thumbnail. Click the layer (name or thumbnail) to paint its pixels, click the chip to paint its mask; the active element carries the blue outline. Ctrl+I inverts the mask, Shift+click the chip disables it, Alt+click the chip views it white on black. While the mask is the target the color panel switches to greys (a black-to-white ramp, hue and saturation dimmed, brightness is the level, five grey swatches): white reveals, black hides, a grey reveals partially (so D then X flip between the two), the eraser hides, the bucket follows the same rule, and pressure, softness and selections apply as usual. With the mask active, the 🗑 deletes the mask and leaves the layer; select the layer itself to delete the layer. A group's mask applies to everything inside it as one. Masks move with their layer and are stored as files like paint layers; the row menu also offers reveal all, hide all, disable and remove. Groups: Ctrl+click rows to select several, Ctrl+G (or the folder button in the tray) folds them into a group (one level of folders, like a sketch needs), Ctrl+Shift+G dissolves the selected group. The folder row hides or shows its children as one, folds with the chevron, and moves as a block. Dragging a layer onto a group's child puts it in the group, dragging it onto a top-level layer takes it out. Groups are organization only: the flattened image is the same with or without them. Under the stack, the wired images tray: click one to add it as a layer (it lands fitted and centered; add it twice for two copies). Wheel zooms (past 1.5× the preview switches to full native resolution), middle-drag pans. ? (or the keyboard button at the bottom of the rail) shows the full shortcut table inside the editor. ✓ Use this sketch uploads the painted layers, flattens the stack and puts the result on the node: the image plug is live immediately. The node has no ▶ of its own: it is the door to the editor, and any run downstream re-uses the flatten for free until you edit again.

The one paid thing in the Sketchpad, and the reason the sketch exists: a generation layer turns your marks into a photoreal render, in place, without leaving the editor. Sketch the intent on a paint layer: where the thing goes, how big, roughly what shape, which colors. A forest, a sword, a piece of cloth can never be drawn in detail, and they do not have to be. Then press the ✦ button in the layer tray (next to +): with a paint layer selected it makes a generation layer that follows that layer; with anything else selected it makes a general one that follows every painted layer below it. (Also: Ctrl+Enter, or right-click a paint layer → ✦ Generate from this layer…) The new layer lands right above, its row shows ↳ and what it follows, and the properties bar becomes the layer's own, one row: ↳ follows: one paint layer, a previous generation (iterate on a take: "make the lake frozen" over the lake you just rendered, its visible region is the guide), all paint below, or whole scene below (rework): no marks at all, the flattened picture under the layer is the subject and the prompt changes it as a whole ("turn this image to winter, same character, same clothes"), generation layers included. A rework is always the whole frame, has no follow setting, and shows entirely (paint a mask if you want to keep parts of the original). Change the choice any time; the prompt: what the marks stand for ("a weathered oak bench", "a pine forest at low sun"); scope: whole frame / local. Whole frame sends the entire canvas and fits the take back to it. Local sends only the marks' region: their bounding box plus some room, extended to a clean aspect ratio (3:2, 16:9, and so on), never cropped into the marks. The model reworks that region at its size tier and the take is scaled back into place, up or down. This is how a 5000 px document stays a 5000 px document: nothing ever regenerates it whole, and you can edit it region by region at full production resolution. Canvases above 2048 px on the long side start in local; pick a size tier at or above the region's long side and the take lands without upscaling. The last region is drawn dashed on the canvas while the layer is selected, and the price dialog states its size and aspect before you pay; follow: loose / balanced / close, how strictly the marks bind. Balanced (the default) makes placement, size and extent binding and leaves the outline, materials and detail to the model. Close makes the silhouette follow the painted shape. Loose treats the marks as a suggestion of placement and size; the model bar: provider, image→image model (the default is GPT Image 2.5 Flare at high), size tier, quality, the ⇄ chip when the model runs through an aggregator, and the price of one render; ✦ Generate. The price is asked first, every time. Nothing renders on its own. The line under the canvas says where the layer stands. The model renders what your marks stand for where they are: their size, roughly their shape and colors, at the strictness you chose, in the scene's light, perspective, scale and grain, with the shadows and reflections it would really cast. The marks themselves disappear from the render. The render comes back whole-frame: the model may change what your object implies anywhere in the picture (a forest at low sun casts long shadows across the whole image). What you see of it is decided by the layer's mask, which is seeded from your marks: the sketched region plus some breathing room, feathered wide. So by default the untouched scene stays pixel-faithful, and you paint the mask white to reveal more of the take: the long shadow, the reflection on the floor, the disturbed sand. Reveal all if the model reworked the scene well as a whole. The mask never re-renders anything: the raster holds the whole frame, painting is free. The row menu offers Re-seed the mask from the sketch when you have redrawn the guide. Generate into a selection. Nothing needs to be drawn: make a selection (marquee, ellipse or lasso, or Ctrl+A) and press ✦ (or Ctrl+Enter). The new layer says ↳ into the selection: the selection becomes its mask (with a soft edge of a few pixels), the model works from the flattened scene below it, and the prompt says what goes there ("a red sports car", "a wet cobblestone patch"). The selection itself is consumed; the layer keeps its outline, which the region-outline button on the bar shows dashed on the canvas (off by default), and re-rolls, staleness and takes work as for any generation layer. Scope defaults to local: the region sent out is the selection plus some room, so the model works on what you selected; switch to whole frame when the prompt names the place itself. There is no follow dial: with no marks, placement is the selection. An ellipse selection on the lawn, the spark, 'add a pond with lush vegetation': the render lands inside the selection only **🕘 takes** on the bar lists every render this layer ever made, from the project ledger. **Use this take** brings any of them back as the layer's raster, fitted into the region it was rendered for, your mask kept, free; it shows as stale if the sketch or the prompt changed since. A re-roll is never destructive. The node face counts stale generation layers. The row says where the layer stands: not rendered, stale (the sketch below it, the prompt or the model changed since the take), done, rendering…, or failed with the provider's reason. A stale layer keeps showing its last take until you generate again; a take that still matches is free (Generate does nothing new). ↻ next to Generate asks for a fresh take of the same sketch and prompt, paying again. Every render is a normal generation on the ledger, with the layer named on the row. A rendered layer behaves like an image layer: eye, opacity, a mask you can paint, Transform. Its take is stored on the node the moment it lands, so closing the editor with Cancel never loses a paid render; ✓ Use this sketch flattens the stack with the generation layers in place. While a layer renders, its row carries the same travelling light as a running node on the canvas. Later: per-layer history and re-pin, and Generate-all-stale from ▶. A new Sketchpad opens with the first wired image already placed as the bottom layer and an empty paint layer selected, so you can draw right away.
From a flat picture: Decompose into layers

A Sketchpad can also start from a finished image. Right-click any picture → Decompose into layers… sends it to Seedream 5.0 (Flash or Pro, on your own BytePlus key), which splits it into a base (the scene with the elements lifted out and the gaps filled in) and up to 16 layers with transparency. Brut lands them as a new Sketchpad beside the picture: the base at the bottom, at the canvas size; every layer above it in the model's stacking order, scaled into its place in the picture and named by the model ("sky", "pavilion", "foreground trees"). Hover a name for the model's description of it; the original on top, hidden: click its eye to compare the recomposed stack with what you started from, or mask it to paint the original back. They are ordinary image layers: move, scale and rotate them with Transform, hide them, give them masks, paint between them, add a generation layer over the stack, and Export PSD carries all of it to Photoshop. The node shows the recomposed picture straight away, and its image plug is live. The model lifts each element out whole (a tree that stood behind a hedge can come back with its full trunk): a layer mask hides what should stay behind. Find in ledger on the node's preview shows the paid run. It is one paid call, and the price is asked first: a form for the model, the size and (optionally) what to separate, then the price dialog with the ceiling. The models, the rates and the size rule are on the Seedream page. Without the BytePlus key the menu item stays greyed with the reason. Right-click a render, Decompose into layers: the price, then a Sketchpad with the pergola, the bench, the building and each tree as its own layer ## Export PSD, for the old schoolers Export PSD in the editor's footer, or right-click the node's preview → Export PSD…, writes a Photoshop file into the project's outputs/exports folder (no dialog; Explorer shows it). Every layer goes in, hidden ones included: paint, placed images and generation takes as raster layers at their placement (moves, scales and rotations baked), layer masks as Photoshop layer masks (feather and invert baked, since PSD has no such switches), groups as folders with their own masks, names, opacity, visibility and color labels. The merged image is the flatten you see on the node. Photoshop, Affinity, Krita and GIMP open it. The export is local and free; the file is written by Brut itself, no library in between.

Painting, layers and the flatten are local and free: no provider call, no ledger row. Only a generation layer's render is a paid call, always behind the price gate. Paint layers, masks and renders are stored as files in the project's outputs, so the graph stays small and a .brutpack or a NAS-rooted project carries the sketch along. Wired images enter as references to their file, not copies. If an upstream node regenerates, the layer keeps pointing at the file it was placed from; add the new image from the tray when you want it. Sketchpad or Layers? Sketchpad makes an image by hand (draw, place, arrange) to generate from. Layers reconciles finished images by painting clipping masks between versions. Use Sketchpad before the generation, Layers after it. Next: an importer for your own Photoshop .abr brush sets may follow.

Where Brut stops being a one-image-at-a-time tool. Multi-Shot explores a scene from many angles at once; the boards are the surfaces where you review, curate and route the results. Every board shares one review gesture: hover a tile and click its 🔍 to open the lightbox — the image fitted to your screen, wheel-zoom into the pixels, and ←/→ (or the on-screen arrows) paging through the whole board like a classical gallery. Clicking the image itself does nothing (no accidental tabs while panning the canvas); the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

A POV/composition explorer. Wire your base image(s) into a Multi-Shot node, pick an exploration scenario and a shot count, and a planner (Gemini, seeing all your base images) writes N distinct shot prompts. Then N image-to-image jobs fill a contact sheet on a resizable node — a worker pool runs several at a time. One scene, one scenario, Run: the contact sheet fills in as the shots land in parallel - **Scenarios** ship as data — Editorial, Ballsy, Morning → Evening, Four Seasons, Dutch Masters, and a **`custom`** scenario that takes its brief from the node's **Notes** field. (Older climate scenarios — Cold North, Mediterranean, Desert — are retired: their weather registers now live as V2 deck cards. A saved graph that used one keeps working and shows it honestly as *retired*.) - **Notes live on the node** — a text box right under the scenario picker steers the planner on any scenario, and for `custom` it *is* the brief. Wired text (a Prompt or Refine node into the notes input) still works and both flow to the planner — wire when the text has a life of its own, type when it's a one-off. Pair `custom` with the *Scenario maker* Refine preset for a strong brief. - **💾 Save as preset** appears under non-empty notes — it saves the text as a **prompt preset** in the global library, loadable from any Prompt node in any project. - **Multi-Shot explores points of view — the look comes after.** For grade/style transfer, don't feed a look reference into the exploration (a former *reference* inlet did exactly that and was retired: it pulled every composition toward the reference and made sheets repetitive). Instead, run the shots you keep through a **Compose** node: *scene* = the shot, *reference* = the look image, prompt = the built-in **Grade match** preset ("use the color grading of the second image…"). You pay once per keeper instead of per exploration, and 1-to-1 transfer is far stronger. - **Plan caching** — the shot list is cached on its own, so stable prompts keep per-shot caches working. **🎲** rolls a new shot list. - **Per-tile controls** — **↻** re-rolls one tile (only that tile re-pays), **✓ / ✗** mark keepers and misses, **🕘** re-pins a past result for that specific tile. - **Curation flows downstream** — ✓ shots flow out the main port (or all non-✗ if none are ticked), taking effect on the next cached run. The contact sheet uses a tidy, deterministic column count from the shot count (≤4 → 2×2, ≤9 → 3-wide, else 4-wide), so it stays neat at any node size. The node's corner grip sets its width only: the height always follows the content — the Notes box (eight lines minimum, drag its own corner for more), the controls and the sheet's rows of squares — so the tiles are never squashed. The eye button beside New shot list folds the sheet away (the shots are kept, the node shrinks to its controls; the Shot Board is the place to review them large).

New Multi-Shot nodes plan with V2; a small V1/V2 rollout next to the title switches generations (existing graphs stay on V1, the original planner frozen for honest comparison). V2 keeps your sheets from repeating the same ideas job after job — the same prop, the same weather trick: The card deck. Every plan draws a hand of ingredients from the scenario's pools (a light register, a life event, a prop domain, …) for the set to use. The hand is shown as chips on the node before you ever run — visible surprise — and the little 🎲 beside the chips redraws it without starting a run. Pick your hand. Random is the default, but the ✎ beside the chips opens the picker: one row per pool, each set to random or a card of your choice. Pinned cards always ride the hand (shown as accent chips; wild cards are pickable at any dial level), the Surprise dial fills the remaining slots randomly, and 🎲 redraws only those. Pin everything — or pin on Classic, which draws nothing on its own — and the hand is fully yours. Picks belong to their scenario's deck, so switching scenario clears them. The Surprise dial. Classic (no cards — the calm grammar brief alone) · Fresh (the default hand) · Crazy (a bigger hand including each pool's wild cards, plus a push toward the never-published). Avoid recent motifs (off by default). Brut remembers the distinctive ideas of your recent plans, per scenario and across all projects. Tick the box and new plans steer away from them — the direct cure for "the same idea on every job". The memory ages out, so retired classics eventually return. The Surprise dial deals cards, 🎲 redraws the random slots, ✎ pins the ones you want to keep V2 also makes the **planner model selectable** — the text model that writes the shot list (the node's Provider/Model picks stay the *image* model that renders them). The default is **Gemini 3.8 Flash**; different planners have different instincts, which is itself a variety lever, and models with a reasoning dial expose it here too. Should a planner's reply come back broken, Brut retries the planning call once before failing loudly — the Activity panel notes the retry. Planning calls cost cents; nothing is rendered until the shot list is valid.

The review surface for a Multi-Shot node. Wire the Multi-Shot shots output into a Shot Board and get a large captioned grid — the prompt under each image, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ proxied to the source. Each tile has its own output plug (shot-<i>) so you can route one chosen shot into Compose or Image→Video. The board re-emits the curated pool from its bottom port. Tiles show each shot at its real aspect (a 9:16 batch is a column of portrait frames, never a 4:3 crop); the Multi-Shot node's own compact sheet stays square thumbnails — the board is where you judge the actual frame. Accept and reject on big tiles, then wire one shot out of its own plug into Image to Video ## Reference Board Makes the crew's stills pool visible. Every image you wire in becomes a numbered tile — and the tile number is the global still number the cinema agents refer to, which kills the invisible wire-order problem. The crew's stills pool made visible: the tile number is the still number the agents use - **↑ / ↓** reorder (the plan refers to the stills by number, so reordering changes what a wire carries — WYSIWYG). - **✕** hide a tile / **↺** restore it in place. - Per-tile `ref-` output plugs address one still by its board number. Free and local — it's just a lens on the images you already have.

The cinema planning nodes: they read your stills and pass a plan document (JSON on a text wire) toward Film Shots. Planning runs on the LLM you choose — Gemini, GPT or Claude — on your own key; on models with a reasoning dial (GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Sol / Luna, details; Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8 / Opus 5 / Opus 5.5, details) a Reasoning select appears — deeper thinking for harder plans, billed as output tokens. For the end-to-end story, see the Cinema Sessions walkthrough. The chain is: stills → Director → Storyboard → Film Shots. (The original four-agent crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor — is legacy, kept at the bottom of this page.)
The Director — the whole crew in one node

One agent that plans the whole film: it analyzes your stills, writes the concept, the look and the executable shot plan, and wires straight into the Storyboard. The anchors it writes use the numbers you see on the Reference Board. The plan comes out varied: an arc across the film, framing, lens, camera height and movement changing shot to shot, and no still overused. Its dials: a Brief (what film) and a Style (what look) from the same libraries the crew uses, the shot count and runtime, a People dial (none / subtle / lively), and an Audio switch that has every clip carry a one-line ambient sound note (used only by video models that produce sound). The plan it writes also carries a concept paragraph: the film's emotional tone, arc, lighting mood and pacing, readable and editable in 📖 Review like everything else. Advanced dials — locked production choices. The Advanced disclosure exposes six craft dials: Camera (RED digital / ARRI / Sony Venice / Blackmagic / IMAX / 35mm / 16mm film), Lenses (clean primes / anamorphic / vintage / long-lens compression), Lighting, Composition, Emphasis and Movement (contemplative → kinetic). Each pick is binding and wins over the style where they disagree; every dial defaults to Director's choice, which adds nothing. The proof sheet is always ONE image, and it renders in the run. Running the Director renders the sheet right after the plan (the whole film as a single contact sheet, at the price on the bar) and opens the review: the sheet large, the frame chips, and your call — Take this sheet (the run goes on; a later run whose sheet is unchanged never asks again), ↻ New take (a fresh render of the same plan, paying again), ✎ Reinvent the ✗ frames (the sheet re-renders for the new plan, the review stays open), or Stop (nothing downstream runs, nothing more is spent). An unchanged plan replays its sheet from cache, free; a render that fails offers to go on without a sheet. The sheet's shape follows its grid: ten 16:9 frames render as two columns of five on a 3:4 sheet, so every frame keeps the film's shape instead of stretching wide (an aspect you set on the bar wins). 🎬 Proof on the face still renders by hand, ⤢ Review reopens the review, 🕘 opens every sheet the film ever rendered, from the project ledger, and 📌 pins one — a pinned sheet stays the film's validated sheet (and keyframe reference) through plan edits and new takes, until unpinned, and a run never asks about a pinned sheet. Inside a closed card (the Stills → Film workflow) the same review opens over the canvas, the card carries a 🎬 Proof sheet button to reopen it and a 📖 Plan button that opens this same document review for the Director inside; the image model of the sheet and of the keyframes is pinned on the card (GPT Image 2.5 Flare, xhigh at 2K) and changed by opening it. The node's Setup, plan and Proof sheet sections all collapse to keep the card compact. Your own brief and style are wires, not notes. The node has two labeled text inlets — brief (optional) and style (optional) — made for a Prompt node (whose text is saveable as a preset, or refined through a Refine). A wired brief composes with the select: the canned entry sets the genre, your wire carries the project's specifics, and where they conflict the wire wins — the node says "⇄ wired in" under the select so the precedence is never invisible. For a fully custom film, set the select to None and let the wire direct alone. The Notes box is just notes: extra guidance, always honored, never secretly the brief. The proof sheet — see the whole film for cents. Below the plan, the Director carries the sheet's bar (pick the image model, size and quality; cheap settings are fine, this is for your eyes): ONE image generation renders the entire film as a numbered contact sheet — every frame, one shared grade — from your stills and the plan's prompts. Judge it, then ✗ the frames that fail (the chips match the sheet's number badges) and hit ✎ Reinvent — one planning call rewrites only the rejected clips with genuinely new compositions; every kept clip stays exactly as it was. The sheet re-renders for cents; loop until the film reads right. The spend ladder is the point: ~1¢ of plan → ~6¢ of proof → keyframes → clips, and you never pay the next tier until the previous one convinced you — which is why the run itself stops on the sheet and waits for your call. The validated sheet then directs the keyframes. When a Storyboard downstream generates an invented shot's keyframe, it follows that frame of the sheet (composition, light, grade) at full resolution, while your stills keep the building true. A new sheet means the unpinned keyframes render again: what you validated is what gets produced. Every keyframe also carries the film's look, sheet or no sheet, so frames generated separately read as one film. (The sheet itself is never cropped into a frame: its resolution is for your eyes only.) It emits the exact same plan document as the legacy DoP chain, so everything downstream is identical: the Storyboard, keyframes, end frames, Film Shots, Review and Revise.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor

Legacy since 1.1.1. The Director plans better films than the four-agent chain. The crew nodes are therefore hidden from the node browser — but they remain fully functional: every saved graph that uses them keeps loading and running, Review/Revise included. New films should start from the Director (or the Cinema Director library template).
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Scenarist

Writes the treatment — the story and beat structure — from your stills. You pick a brief (or custom, where your notes are the brief). Each shot stays on one still, so grounding stays honest. It may also invent shots — compositions no still contains (detail close-ups, reveals, human presence, pull-back endings; the Cinematic Reel (flourish) brief leans into this). An invented shot names the stills that anchor it and carries a written keyframe prompt; Brut generates that missing frame from your stills on the Storyboard before any video runs, so the identity never drifts. A still grounds at most two shots, never back to back, and the "Invent every shot" switch goes all the way: stills become references only, every start frame generated.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Artistic Director

Sets the look: a style bible and per-shot art direction — palette, lighting, mood. Choose a style (or custom). It builds on the Scenarist's treatment. On invented shots it also styles the keyframe prompt (palette, light, lens character) — composing the frame is exactly its job.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › DoP (Director of Photography)
Turns the treatment into an executable shot plan — the camera language, motion, and which still grounds each shot, as a concrete list of clips with durations. This is the plan Film Shots executes.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Script Supervisor
The continuity pass: harmonizes speed, light and palette across all the clips so the sequence feels like one film, not a pile of clips. It never changes which still a shot stands on.

Not an agent but the crew's review surface. The Storyboard turns the plan into an editable board of shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, dynamic position badges. It emits concrete image paths, so Film Shots downstream only needs the plan wire. ✕ mutes, it never deletes. A muted card stays on the board, greyed and badged muted, out of the film: its keyframes, pins and prompts are kept, the position badges renumber around it, and ↺ on the card (or ↺ N muted in the header) brings it back in place. Only a hand-added shot can be deleted for good (🗑, once muted). The same discipline as the Shot Board's ✗: a clip you cut is a clip you can still see. Wrong still numbers never pass silently. When a plan's still numbers are off by one in an obvious way, Brut corrects them and says so in the Activity panel; any other number the board can't serve fails loudly on its card. Invented shots arrive frameless with a 🎨 Generate keyframe button: a render from the shot's anchor stills at the film's aspect (cents, priced on the board next to the image-model picker). Keyframes cache on their prompt + anchors, ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins, 🕘 opens the card's history — every keyframe it ever generated, from the project ledger, any past take re-pinnable as the start frame for free — a wired image overrides, and the start selector can still ground the shot on a real still instead (🎨 generate in the same selector brings the keyframe back). The 🎨 entry is on every card: a grounded shot, or a shot you added with +, switches to a generated keyframe of its own. Write its keyframe prompt (✏, the 🎨 line), check its anchor stills (the still the card was on, by default; empty = every still on the board), 🎨. An invented shot with no keyframe blocks that clip in Film Shots — it is never silently sent as text-to-video; a card whose keyframe prompt is still to write says so and stays blocked the same way. Swap a start frame, generate a keyframe for an invented shot, drag a frame out to keep it The board also owns the **film's aspect ratio**: a dropdown (defaulting to the plan's format) that conforms every keyframe and travels in the emitted plan. Changing it re-crops the kept raw renders for free — no regeneration. ▶ on the board batch-renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation (count, per-frame price, total); the per-card 🎨 stays for one-offs. Its companion ↻ New takes re-rolls every generated keyframe at once — fresh takes on the current model, each paying again, one itemized confirm — for a model switch or a general do-over; 📌 pinned, wired and grounded cards are kept, and old takes stay pinnable in each card's 🕘 history. A prompts on/off switch declutters the cards, and the whole pre-wired chain ships as the Cinema Crew library template (File ▾ → Browse library…). End frames, on demand. Each card's end selector is none · a still · 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right — same image box, own in-socket and out-plug, own tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame, at the film's aspect. Its prompt is drafted for you from the start frame, the shot's move and the reference board, with up to three stills picked to show what the move reveals (one text call on the planning model of the node feeding the plan); ✎ / 🎨 open a review — start frame beside the editable draft, ✎ re-drafts, the still picks as toggleable thumbnails, Generate renders — so nothing renders from a prompt you haven't read. ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins (surviving prompt edits and a re-rolled start; otherwise a new start orphans its end), 🕘 = the end frame's history. ▶ on the board reviews every armed card in one modal after the start keyframes. An armed end frame still pending blocks its clip downstream; a video model without an end-frame input runs the clip from the start alone and the Film Shots table says so on that row. Every frame block is also a source: the plug on its image edge carries that frame — the start frame (keyframe, wired image or grounded still) or the end frame — and a pending frame delivers nothing; the labeled plug bar at the card's bottom carries the clip's final prompt (overrides and wired prompts applied; in on the left, out on the right), an invented shot's keyframe prompt (its own in pin on the left too: wire a Refine output or a Text Board tile and it becomes the generated frame's prompt, a new keyframe) and the validated end prompt, for reuse or refinement anywhere. Card images can be dragged straight onto the canvas to detach into a ready-filled Image In.
📖 Review — read it like a document, direct it like a director

The raw JSON on the node face is for the wire, not for you. Every crew node has a 📖 Review button that opens the document as a document: the title as a headline, the analysis as prose, the style bible as labeled sections, every shot a numbered card with its prompt, camera, duration and grounding badges. Two verbs live in that modal, with two costs: Edit — free. Every text field is editable in place. Save writes each field back into the same place in the document, so the structure the downstream chain depends on can never drift; it behaves exactly like hand-editing the node's text, just humane. Anchors are editable too. An invented shot's card shows its anchor stills (the 0-based still numbers its keyframe is built from) as a small list you can rewrite: 0, 3. The field knows how many stills the node is wired to and flags any number the board can't serve, so a stray anchor is a two-second fix instead of a re-plan. 💬 Comment → Revise — one planning call (cents, ledgered). Every section and shot card takes a margin note ("shot 4 slower", "the whole film should feel like dusk"), plus an overall-notes box. Revise with comments hands the agent its own document and your notes; it returns the same document revised — same shot ids, same structure, only what your notes require changed — and the comments clear once addressed. A revision that would break the document's structure is rejected and your document stays untouched. Comments survive closing the modal, and the node's Review button shows how many are waiting. The plan as a document; a margin note on one shot, Revise, and only that changes They compose: fix wording directly, comment the conceptual asks, revise — the revision starts from your edited text.

Agent output is editable text. Hand-edit a plan and your changes flow downstream while inputs are unchanged; change an input or roll again (🎲) and the agent regenerates over your edits — deliberately. The planner sees your stills (downscaled for the model's request cap; generation always gets full resolution), and its analysis shows in the Activity panel. The plan you approve is the film you get. Every clip starts from a frame you have seen (a still of yours, or a keyframe generated from your stills), a shot without its frame never rolls, and every clip asks for a steady camera.
→ Video — shoot the plan, review the clips, cut the sequence.
Where stills become motion. Brut treats video like the expensive thing it is — every clip is quoted and confirmed before a cent is spent.

The footer of every video node reads the clip's size, duration and frame rate (1920 × 1080 · 5.0 s · 24 fps) at the bottom left, on the output pin's row. Animate a single image into a clip. Wire an image into the node, pick a provider and model, set duration/resolution and (where supported) audio and an end frame, and run. Pick the model and duration, read the estimate, run, and the clip plays on the node Providers: **Kling** (REST and subscription), **Google Veo**, **Gemini Omni**, and **Seedance** — see [Providers](/docs/providers/index.html). Some models do text-to-video too. The node shows a **cost estimate before you run**, derived from Brut's data-driven pricing. Clip length follows the model: Kling and Veo offer a few fixed durations, Gemini Omni 3–10 s, Seedance 2.5 anything from 4 to 30 s (or smart, where the model picks). Some models tie the two selects together: on Google Veo, 1080p and 4K render at 8 s only and reference images need 8 s, so the picks that cannot go together grey out in place with the reason, and a ⚠ line under the selects says what to change; where the provider's endpoint takes no audio switch (Veo on your Google key), the audio box shows ticked and greyed (the rules). On models whose clip must keep the start frame's aspect ratio (Seedance 2.5), the aspect select disappears while a start frame is wired and the node says so; the request is sent the way the provider demands. With nothing on the image inlet the run is text-to-video and the aspect select is back, since that run takes a ratio of your choice. Ratio: follow the input. The aspect menu's first entry follows the start frame: when you run, Brut measures the wired image and sends the provider's nearest ratio (a 2048 × 1143 still goes out as 16:9, a portrait one as 9:16), so the clip keeps the frame you composed instead of being stretched or banded to a fixed ratio. Steady camera asks the model for one smooth, stabilized move with no shake and no drift, as Film Shots does for every clip. Running a finished node again replays its clip from cache, free. Want another take of the same shot? The title bar's ↻ re-roll generates a fresh one (billed again, at the same estimate); the previous clip stays in the node's 🕘 history, pinnable.

Tick Draft take and the node renders a 480p draft, billed like any 480p clip. When the draft is the shot you want, ⬆ Render final 1080p re-renders the same shot at 1080p from the draft's task id: BytePlus reuses the prompt, the frames, the references, the duration, the seed and the audio, nothing is re-sent, and the final is billed like any 1080p clip, after the usual confirm with its price. The final then replaces the draft on the node and on every wire (the footer line reads 1920 × 1080), while the draft stays in the node's 🕘 history. A re-roll or a changed prompt starts a new draft, and the old final stays in the ledger like every paid file. A draft can be finalized for seven days; the node's line says until when. Explore at 480p, pay 1080p only for keepers. Draft mode needs your own BytePlus key: a node running through an aggregator shows no Draft box. Last frame (Seedance). Seedance returns every clip's final frame as an image, at the clip's exact size, and Brut keeps it beside the clip. ⏭ Last frame → Image In under the result drops it on the canvas as an Image In: wire it into the next Image → Video's start frame and the shot continues where this one ended. When a final was rendered from a draft, the button gives the final's last frame. The trust line (Seedance). BytePlus refuses a wired picture that looks like a real person unless one of its own models made it on your key. The node reads the ledger for every wired picture, the start frame, the end frame and each reference, and says in green which ones carry that trust, with the day the 30-day window closes: made on your BytePlus key: start frame, references 1, 2. A picture counts when it is a Seedream text-to-image result or a Seedance clip's last frame. When the same set also holds pictures Seedance will refuse a face in (a Seedream edit, a picture from another model), an amber line names them, so a refusal is visible before the run. A picture with no line either way is one Brut cannot trace (an upload, a Conform cut): that is no verdict. A node fed only by other makers' pictures shows no line at all. When a video model runs through an aggregator route (the "⇄ runs via …" chip — e.g. Kling v3 on your OpenRouter key), the node shows only the knobs that route actually accepts: settings the aggregator doesn't carry (like the aspect-ratio select or the negative prompt on OpenRouter's Kling) disappear rather than fail the run. The clip's aspect still follows the start frame you wire in. Add the native key to get the full control set back.

Some models accept extra reference images alongside the start frame — a character, a product, a style plate — and keep them consistent in the clip. When the selected model supports them, the node grows a references inlet and its info line says so ("✓ takes reference images (up to N)"); models that don't say that too, so you never guess. A Reference Board plugs straight in — its numbered tiles (or the whole curated pool) wire onto the inlet. Current support: Seedance 2.5 (up to 30, addressed as @Image1… in the prompt), Gemini Omni Flash, Kling o1 / 3.0 Omni (subscription, up to 6), Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1 / 3.1 Fast (up to 3). Wiring references into a model that can't take them fails with a clear message — Brut never silently drops an image you wired.
Film Shots — the cinema batch executor

Film Shots takes a shot plan (from the Director / Storyboard) and shoots the whole sequence. Prompts written for the model you picked. Before a clip is shot, Film Shots adapts the Director's prompt to the video model you picked (Kling, Seedance, Veo or Omni), so each model gets the kind of prompt it follows best. A cheap text model does it, one call per clip. There is nothing to set: the table marks rewritten rows with ✦ (hover one to read the Director's text under the rewrite), the confirmation says how many were written, and the activity log carries each call. Rewrites are cached per clip: an unchanged plan never calls again, a plan edit rewrites that clip, and picking a model of another family rewrites every prompt on the next run (the clips then roll again, as a new model would anyway). A rewrite that fails is said out loud on the row and in the confirmation, and that clip goes out with the Director's text. Its defining feature is the cost guard: It prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, estimated cost — and shows an itemized confirmation before any spend. Cancel a line and the total updates. Tick boxes choose what gets sent. Every row has one, all ticked by default; untick a clip and it stays in the table, greyed, not sent, not priced, not in the output pool — generate three, judge them, then tick the rest. The Σ row's box ticks or unticks everything, and its N of M clips line always says what Generate would actually send. Ticks are saved with the graph (never in library recipes). Cached and pinned clips cost $0 and are never re-quoted. A ruled resolution snaps the plan's durations. Veo renders 1080p at 8 s only: with 1080p picked, every clip in the table becomes 8 s, the line under the Resolution select says so, and the confirm lists the 8 s rows. A row that still breaks a rule is blocked with the fix, like an invented shot without its keyframe. It fans out on a worker pool (staggered to respect provider rate limits), with the same per-clip semantics as Multi-Shot: cache / ↻ re-roll / ✓✗ verdicts / 📌 pins. On Kling (subscription) without a subscription, kling.ai runs one clip at a time and watermarks it: clips refused for that reason wait and run one by one after the pool, the row saying so on hover, the Activity panel saying why once. Every clip asks for a steady camera, and a clip gets sound only when you switch audio on and the model makes sound. An invented shot whose keyframe hasn't been generated on the Storyboard is a per-clip error — that clip is blocked (and counted in the confirm), never silently downgraded to text-to-video. The rest of the batch rolls normally. A shot added on the Storyboard with no clip prompt yet is listed and blocked the same way, the row naming the fix, instead of vanishing from the table. Draft mode on Seedance 2.5: tick Draft takes and every clip rolls at 480p, billed like 480p. Once the drafts are in, each row grows a final 1080p tick; ⬆ Render N finals re-renders exactly those shots at 1080p from their draft task ids, after its own itemized confirm. A finalized row's output becomes the final, on the Clip Board and in the Sequence downstream, while the draft stays in 🕘. Seven days to finalize a draft; your own BytePlus key only. Every clip priced in the table, one itemized confirmation, nothing spends before your OK Nothing is generated until you confirm the total. That confirm no longer freezes the rest of a running graph — other branches keep working while it waits. Like Image → Video, a routed model (the "⇄ runs via …" chip) shows only the knobs its route accepts — the quote table and the clips both use exactly what will be sent, and the film's aspect rides each clip's start frame.

The review board for Film Shots — video tiles, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ per clip, and per-tile clip-<i> plugs to route one clip onward. The video equivalent of the Shot Board. Tiles show a still poster of each clip (in the clip's own aspect ratio) and stay feather-light — press ▶ on a tile to play it; one clip plays at a time, and 🔍 opens it full-screen — ←/→ screens the whole board clip by clip. The /row select goes up to 15, so a whole reel can sit in one row.

Wire your curated clips into a Sequence node and it assembles them into one mp4 with local ffmpeg — cuts or chained crossfades, scaled and padded to a common size. It's free, cached, and needs no ledger. Two clips cut together with a crossfade and played in Preview: local ffmpeg on your machine, no cost - ffmpeg ships as a static binary inside Brut (no system install). - The film **follows the first clip's orientation** — a pool of vertical 9:16 clips assembles into a vertical reel, not a pillarboxed landscape frame. The Quality select sets the short side (1080p vertical = 1080 wide). - **Clip audio is kept.** Clips with native sound (Veo, Seedance, Kling with audio on) carry it into the film; silent clips get exact-length silence so nothing drifts; crossfades fade the audio too. A pool with no sound anywhere produces a clean video-only file.
The video nodes are the back half of the Cinema Sessions: Storyboard → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview. Read that walkthrough to see them working together.

Upscalers grow an image to delivery resolution — the finishing step after you've generated and curated. They are paid nodes: the source image goes to the upscaling provider with your own key, and cost scales with output pixels, not input.

Wire one image in (from Image In, any generator, a Shot Board tile…), pick a model, run. The upscaled image flows out the bottom port like any other image — into a Preview, a Conform, or straight to disk via the ledger. Batch: wire several images (an Image In folder, a curated Shot Board pool) and each one upscales as its own job — two in parallel, with a per-image cache, so a re-run only pays for what changed and a partial failure retries just the failures. The estimate line sums the whole set, and each output's 🔍 compares against its input. Caching works as everywhere: unchanged input + unchanged dials = free replay; the 🕘 history lets you re-pin any past result. The node shows a live estimate — input size → output size, megapixels, and the approximate cost — before you spend anything. A preset, a live estimate, run, then the before/after wipe zoomed into the brickwork ### Models (Topaz Labs) Model What it does Gigapixel Standard 2 / High Fidelity 2 / Low Resolution 2 Faithful precision upscaling — no invention, tuned respectively for everyday use, maximum preservation, and tiny sources. Gigapixel Art & CGI Precision upscaling for renders, illustrations and graphics — keeps clean edges and flat color, avoids photographic texture artifacts. The archviz workhorse. Redefine / Standard MAX / Recover 3 Generative enhancement (photoreal, true-to-input, or restoration) with an optional guidance prompt and a 1–9 creativity dial. Topaz bills credits (see the provider page); the node shows your live balance and a per-run credit estimate, and the ledger records the credits each job actually billed.

Model What it does Upscaler Creative The famous "reimagining" upscaler: 2x/4x/8x/16x with a guidance prompt and the creativity / HDR / resemblance / fractality dials, plus an engine choice (Illusio = smooth, Sharpy = crisp, Sparkle = detailed). It invents plausible detail — great for stylized finishes, wrong for strict fidelity. Input capped at 25.3M pixels. Upscaler Precision V2 Faithful, detail-preserving upscale from 2x to 16x with sharpen / smart grain / ultra detail knobs and a flavor per image type: photo, sublime (illustration), photo_denoiser (grainy or low-light sources). The archviz default.

The 🔍 on the node's result opens straight into a full-screen before/after comparison of the input against the upscaled output: drag the divider to sweep between them (the input is shown at the same size, so you're comparing detail, not scale). The mouse wheel zooms — the fast display copy is shown until you zoom, then the original files load so you're judging real pixels — drag pans when zoomed in, double-click resets, Esc or a click outside closes. The same wheel-zoom works in every magnified preview across Brut.

Your favorite dial combinations can be saved as named upscaling presets — the 💾 button next to the preset select stores the current model + dials in Brut's global library (all projects, both dev and installed app). Picking a preset applies it; editing any dial detaches it (your params are always the truth); ✕ deletes it from the library.

The clip finisher: wire one clip in (a Clip Board tile, an Image → Video output, a whole Sequence), pick a provider and model, choose a scale — plain 2x / 4x or a standard target: → HD, → 4K, → 8K (the target sizes the clip's short side, so a portrait 9:16 reel "at 4K" comes out 2160 wide) — and run. The upscaled clip flows out — audio is kept. Two providers, same models: Topaz Labs (cloud) — bills credits per job, works anywhere. Topaz Video AI (local) — free: if you own the Topaz Video desktop app, Brut runs the upscale on your GPU. No key, no credits, no confirm dialog, and the clip never leaves your machine. See the provider page. Nothing bills without your OK — every cloud run opens an itemized confirmation with the credit estimate first (cached and pinned replays never ask; free local runs don't either). Topaz's own analysis is the billing truth: the lower bound of its quote is billed and lands in the ledger. Cloud jobs can take a while on real clips; they run engine-side, survive restarts, and reattach. Local jobs simply re-run if interrupted — nothing was billed. Output caps at 8K per side; cloud uploads at 500MB. Target 4K on the short side, read the itemized confirmation, keep the clip's sound | Model | When | |---|---| | **Proteus 4** | the general-purpose default — upscale, denoise, sharpen in one pass | | **Rhea** | natural-texture enhancement, higher scales | | **Gaia CG** | **rendered/CG clips** — archviz animations, clean edges |

Upscales are priced by output image area (and for video, × duration). Magnific's doc rates work out to roughly €0.025 per output megapixel with a €0.10 minimum — Brut shows this as an approximate $ figure before the run, and the ledger records the estimate from the actual output pixels after it. Rough feel: a 1080p still → 4K is ~€0.20; pushing a 640×480 crop to 16x lands near €2. As everywhere in Brut: your key, your bill, zero markup.
Small, local, free — the glue between generation steps.

Brings stills to one aspect ratio before generation, so a set of mixed-ratio renders becomes a clean, consistent batch (video models in particular want a single ratio). Choose a target aspect ratio and a method: crop trims each still to the ratio. The edges outside the frame are lost; what stays keeps its full resolution. Free. extend takes the still to the new ratio by having a painter paint what the frame adds. A render that must grow from 4:3 to 16:9 without losing the building is the case. The frame is free and applies itself; the paint is the paid step, one call per still: ✦ Paint this still in the ✂ editor paints that one, ✦ Paint N stills on the node paints every pending one, and Run prices them first. Each tile says to paint until it is, then ✦ painted. Per tile, ↻ paints that still again (a fresh take), 🕘 opens every paint of that still from the ledger and 📌 pins a past take, which flows until unpinned or until the frame changes. What flows out of the node is the painted set, never a still that is not painted yet. pad keeps the whole still on blurred, darkened bars of itself, the letterbox look. Free. The node's height follows its tiles: each still shows at its conformed aspect and the node grows or shrinks with them (a 9:16 set makes a tall node, a 21:9 set a flat one); the n / row selector and the width grip are the size controls, there is no inner scrollbar. Per-image ✂ crop editor: drag an aspect-locked rectangle to choose which part of each still survives the conform (the default is a center cut — architecture rarely sits dead-center). The crop is stored per image; the engine crops the original at full resolution. A hand crop always wins over the method for its still. An edge close to the picture's edge snaps to it, a frame close to centered snaps to centered, and Shift while dragging locks the move to one direction. On extend and pad, the same editor places the frame: the stage grows room around the picture and the frame may reach into it. Drag it across the picture to choose which side grows (all of the extension on the right, for instance, or a little above and below as well), the corner scales it, the readout says how many pixels are added. A frame that reaches outside the picture belongs to those two methods: switch back to crop and that still takes the automatic cut again, with the frame kept for the next switch. On extend, the editor also holds the painter: provider, model, output size and, for GPT Image, quality. It starts on FLUX Outpaint when you hold a Black Forest Labs key, on GPT Image 2.5 Flare at xhigh otherwise. The line beside it is the price of painting this one still at this frame. The picks are the node's (every still is painted the same way) and apply at once; the frame and the optional note for the still (what should appear in the added part: more lawn, no new buildings) go with Save frame or ✦ Paint this still. Reset frame puts the frame back on its automatic placement. Two kinds of painter, and they do not behave the same. An outpainting tool holds your picture. FLUX Outpaint (Black Forest Labs) takes the picture and the frame and generates only what the frame adds: the picture stays where you put it. It answers at the frame's size up to 4 megapixels (or up to 2 or 1, your pick: its price follows the size, about $0.10 per megapixel in High; a Fast mode paints in seconds for about $0.05, rougher in the added part); a larger frame is painted smaller (the line under the picture says at what size) and delivered at that size, never scaled back up. Use Upscale Image after it when you need more pixels. It needs no prompt; your note travels as a hint. An image model redraws the frame. GPT Image, Nano Banana, FLUX 3 and Seedream have no fill mode: they are shown your picture on its frame and paint a new picture at that ratio. The result is one coherent image, but it is the model's version of your still: details inside it are re-rendered, and the model may shift or re-proportion the scene. Same as the picture asks for the frame's own size; pick a tier to render the frame's ratio at that size instead. You get the painter's picture, as it is. Brut does not paste your original back over a redraw (a model that moved the scene would leave doubled edges at the seam). When the original must stay pixel for pixel, the outpainting tool is the painter to pick. The prompt is written for each still when the painter is an image model: a cheap text model looks at the picture and writes it for you, your note folded in. One call per still (cents, in the ledger as a planning row), kept until the frame or the note changes, so a fresh take reuses the same words. When no text model can be reached, a short fixed prompt is sent and the Activity panel says so. Free ratio: pick free at the bottom of the Aspect menu when the stills don't need one shared ratio. Each still's ✂ editor then crops freely: drag any corner or edge to any shape, the size in pixels shows under the image. Stills you don't crop pass through as they are, and the Method menu greys out (there is nothing to pick). Crops remember the ratio they were drawn for, so switching back to 16:9 uses your 16:9 crops, never the free ones. No ▶ to press: Conform applies itself. Save a crop, change the ratio, the method or the fill, wire a new still in, and the tiles update on their own. Only the stills that changed are re-cut: the others keep their files, so nothing downstream of them runs again. The stills sit on a resizable board: pick 1 to 5 per row from the n / row selector (never more columns than stills, so a single still fills the node) and drag the node's corner to size the tiles; many stills scroll inside the frame instead of stretching the node into a column. Each image gets its own output plug, so you can route conformed stills individually. Each row's 🔍 opens the lightbox on the conformed result — ←/→ pages the whole set, so you can flip through the batch and check every cut. Extend to 4:3 with FLUX Outpaint: drag the frame where the picture should grow, a note for the new part, Paint: the picture stays as it was, only the added sky is painted Cropping, padding and placing the frame run entirely on your machine (local PIL): **free**, never metered. Only Extend's painting is a paid call, and only when you press Paint.

Inspect any output at screen size. Wire an image or video into a Preview node and it shows inline on a resizable frame, live: whatever is plugged in appears the moment it exists — when you open a saved graph, when an upstream node finishes, when you pin a past take — with nothing to press. There is no ▶ on the node (nothing to run; it is a viewing surface, like Compare). The image inlet displays video too. Hover a tile and its 🔍 opens the lightbox — wheel-zoom, and ←/→ pages through everything on the node. When several images are shown, the ‹ › buttons on each tile reorder them. Preview is the "show me the result" node you'll drop at the end of most branches; the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

Two images, one verdict. Wire any two takes into the A and B inlets — a Gemini attempt against a GPT attempt, an original against an Annotate correction, yesterday's keeper against today's re-roll — and the node shows them side by side, live, without running anything. Hover it and the 🔍 opens the real thing: the before/after wipe slider, both layers sharing one zoom and pan, so you can drag the divider across a facade while zoomed into the brickwork. The slider labels pick up the source nodes' names, so it reads "Image → Image vs Annotate & Correct", not "before vs after". Two takes side by side, then the wipe slider with a shared zoom Each pane carries the same small line as the single-output nodes: the picture's pixel size (`2048 × 1152`), a clip's length and frame rate. Compare is a viewing surface, not a processor — free, local, no output port and no ▶ (there is nothing to run; the tiles follow the wires live — route the winner onward from its source node). It's the generalization of the Upscale node's built-in input-vs-result compare: same slider, any two wires you choose.

Every take a node ever made, on the canvas. Projects grow hundreds of generations and the good one from Tuesday is somewhere in the outputs folder. Wire any generation node's output into the History board (the image inlet takes video nodes too) and the board fills with every take that node ever produced, newest first, straight from the project's generation ledger. Wire several nodes in and the board shows one group per node, in wire order, each headed by the node's name and id, its take count and what it has cost so far. That is the point of the board: it reads as "what is inside this branch", not as a flat pile. Tiles carry the model, the date, the cost and, where it applies, the shot number of a Multi-Shot take, the card of a Storyboard keyframe or the Director's proof sheet. The prompt sits under the caption and in the tooltip. Every tile shows the take at its own aspect: a 9:16 take is a tall tile, a 16:9 take a wide one, never a crop, so a node that changed format mid-way reads truthfully. A tile's 🔍 opens the Magnifier, and ←/→ page through that node's whole history. Video takes play in place: a still poster at rest, click ▶ to play (one tile at a time, so a board of forty clips stays light). 📌 pins on the source node. The pin is exactly the 🕘 re-pin: the take becomes the source node's active output on every run, free, until you unpin it there or here. A pinned tile wears the amber ring. Multi-Shot tiles pin their own shot, Storyboard tiles their own keyframe. The board itself has no output and never runs anything: pins act on the source, so keep the downstream wires on the source node and use the board to choose. Drag an image tile onto the canvas to detach it as a ready-filled Image Input, the same gesture as dragging any preview out of a node. Right-click a tile for Reveal in Explorer, Copy, Export. Filter by model when a node has run on several, pick the tiles per row, ↻ re-reads the ledger (it also refreshes on its own whenever a tracked node finishes a run). Wires through a composite card or a reroute dot resolve to the node that actually generated: the board always shows the generator's own history. Wire two generation nodes into a History board: every take, grouped per node, pin one Free, local, nothing leaves the machine: the ledger is a file in the project folder. The board shows the newest 200 takes per node.

A sticky note for the canvas — annotate your graph the way you'd annotate a whiteboard: intent for future-you, instructions for a teammate opening the project later, review remarks next to the branch they're about. Notes aren't nodes — they're placement tools, living in the rail's Organize section (with Stamp, Group and Composite). Click the rail's sticky-note icon and the note rides your cursor: click the canvas to place it at the default size, or click-and-drag to draw its size (Shift places several, Esc or right-click cancels). While you're placing, the nodes underneath freeze — you can drop a note on top of anything. Double-click to write, click elsewhere to finish. Notes support a light markdown: # heading, - bullet, **bold**, *italic*, `code`. Select a note for the toolbar: five sticky colors, four fonts (Sans / Display / Hand / Mono), text sizes from 11 to 256px, bold and italic, left / center / right alignment, plus resize handles. Display order is fixed so annotations always show: stamps over notes over nodes (selecting anything still brings it to the front). Notes have no ports and never execute — free, local, never sent to any provider as part of a run. Notes travel: they're saved in graphs, templates and composites, so a library template can ship its own usage notes. Tidy moves them with the graph — each note keeps its position relative to the node it sits next to. Marcel reads them. A note sitting next to a node is exactly the kind of intent he should see — ask him about the graph and the notes are part of his picture. He can write them too. Place a note from the rail, pick a paper and a font, drop a stamp next to it ## Stamp A frameless emoji mark — the quickest possible annotation. Click the rail's stamp icon, pick your emoji from the flyout, and it rides your cursor; click to drop it — on empty canvas or right on a node (Shift-click for a trail of them). Drop a ⭐ on the keeper, a 🚧 on the branch under construction, a 💩 on what it deserves. Select a stamp to swap the emoji, resize it by the grip in its corner (like a sticky), or delete it. Free, local, no ports.

Draw on the canvas — made for Wacom people (mouse works too). The rail's Pen icon (or the ring's Pen slice) enters draw mode: sketch freely, pen pressure sets the stroke weight, pick a color (theme ink + the five sticky colors) and a width, Alt-click erases a stroke, and Esc or ✓ finishes — the whole session lands as one frameless drawing you can move, resize (it scales as a unit) and delete like any annotation. Free, local, never sent anywhere. Draw over the canvas; the session becomes one resizable ink node ## Text A clean label — for those who prefer tidy organization over stickies: the same note machinery with the paper removed. No fill, no shadow, just typed words on the canvas — perfect for titling regions of a big graph. The label sizes to its content by default; select it and drag the knob on its left or right edge to set the width (the height always follows the text, so a title never clips; double-click a knob to fit the text again), and the font size is its scale control, up to a poster-sized 256px. It gets the full note toolbar (four fonts, sizes, bold, italic, alignment), and the colors apply to the text itself, with a theme-ink default.

Right-click any empty spot on the canvas and a radial menu opens under your hand — every organize tool one flick away. The center names the ring you're on and clicking it cycles three states: Organize (note · stamp · pen · text · group · composite · add node · tidy) → your most-used nodes (learned from your own placements) → your recent stamps. Nodes land where you right-clicked; the annotation tools (note, stamp, text) hop onto your cursor so you place — or click-drag-size — them exactly like from the rail. Power move: press the right button, drag onto a slice, release — picked, no clicking. The rail keeps every tool too; the ring is just the fast hand. Hold the right button on empty canvas: tools, then your most-used nodes, then stamps; release on a pick --- That's the whole palette. Back to Nodes & graphs for how they run together, or on to the Providers.

Brut is bring-your-own-key. You add a key for each provider you want to use; the engine calls that provider directly, on your key, at their price. Brut never holds a key that bills anyone but you, and never marks up a token.

⚙ Settings on the left rail (or the setup wizard) shows every provider as a card — its role, and one status line — grouped by what it does (generation, aggregators, upscalers). Click a card to paste a key (validated on save); the switch on the card turns a provider off without deleting anything. Keys live in your OS keychain — never in a graph, never sent anywhere but the provider. You can also set them via environment variables before launching the engine. Settings, Providers: one card per provider with its status; the switch turns a provider off without deleting its key, a click opens its key ## The one rule that trips everyone up Image and video models need a billing-enabled key. Free tiers usually have zero generation quota, so your very first call returns a 429 — that's billing not enabled, not throttling. Turn on billing in the provider's console and it clears.

Model routes — native first, aggregator fallback

Some models can also run through an aggregator — a third-party service (like an aggregator subscription or a multi-model API) that resells the same model under its own billing. Brut treats those as routes, with three hard rules: Your direct key always wins. If you hold the native provider's key, the generation goes straight to the provider, exactly as before. Routes only activate for a model when you have no native key but do hold the aggregator's credential. Routing is always visible. A routed model shows a ⇄ runs via … chip on the node, the run confirm says who bills, and the ledger records it. Nothing routes silently. The catalog stays curated. An aggregator credential never adds models to Brut — the model list is exactly the one Brut ships, whatever route serves it. Estimates for routed runs come from the route's own measured price, or are absent; aggregators typically charge a margin over the direct API, and the node says so. A routed node says so on its face: runs via OpenRouter, on your OpenRouter account Availability is resolved once at engine start and re-resolved the moment you add or remove a key — adding an aggregator credential mid-session lights up the routed models immediately. Four route providers ship today: **[OpenRouter](/docs/providers/openrouter.html)** (one key for text + images with Brut's native menus + the whole video set — billed cost recorded per job), **[fal.ai](/docs/providers/fal.html)** (API key — Nano Banana family, GPT Image 2, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1), **[Higgsfield](/docs/providers/higgsfield.html)** (subscription plan credits, browser sign-in — Nano Banana 2, Seedance 2.0) and **[Replicate](/docs/providers/replicate.html)** (API token — Nano Banana Pro/2, GPT Image 2, Kling Omni, Veo 3.1 incl. end frames, Seedance incl. text→video). When several credentials exist, that same order decides. Text models route too: with an OpenRouter key (or, text-only, a fal.ai key) the planning models — Refine, the Multi-Shot planner, the cinema crew, Text→Text — run at pass-through token rates when no native text key exists. Marcel routes through OpenRouter too — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through (verified live), so one OpenRouter key is a complete text seat. Deciding between direct keys and an aggregator? The full pros/cons and a feature-by-feature capability matrix live on Keys vs aggregators.

Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic double as planning models — they power the Refine node and the cinema crew, where you pick which LLM writes your treatment or shot plan. Text models never enter the paid generation queue; they're cheap and separate. Provider errors (4xx/429) are surfaced verbatim on the node — Brut never masks them, so what the provider says is what you see.

Brut is bring-your-own-key at heart: the cheapest, highest-fidelity way to run it is a handful of native provider keys, and nothing Brut does ever adds a markup to them. But not everyone wants to open four provider consoles — so Brut also speaks to aggregators, as routes: your aggregator credential serves models you have no native key for, visibly, at the aggregator's own prices. Three setups cover almost everyone. Pick by what you care about most:
Which path should you pick? › 1. Native keys — pick this if you care about price and control

Gemini + OpenAI + one video provider (+ Anthropic for Marcel's best brain). This is what Brut is built around, and it wins on every axis except setup time: Cheapest per generation, structurally. You pay each provider's list rate, full stop — no reseller margin, no credit fee. At studio volume (hundreds of images, dozens of clips a week) the difference is real money. Every knob of every model: exact inpaint masks (OpenAI), Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance Smart Length, native 4K rates — none of which any aggregator carries. The cost: ~5 minutes per provider console, each with billing enabled.
Which path should you pick? › 2. One OpenRouter key — pick this if you care about simplicity

The 2-minute setup, and since v1.0.8 it's a genuinely complete studio: images with Brut's own size/aspect menus (all four Nano Bananas, GPT Image 2), the video set (Kling 3.0 std/pro and O1, Veo 3.1/Fast/Lite with end frames, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5), every planning model, and Marcel — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through so long conversations cost the same as on a native key. A unique honesty bonus: OpenRouter reports the exact billed cost of every job, and Brut writes it straight onto your ledger. The two-minute setup: one OpenRouter card configured, every other card empty, most of Brut lit up What you give up: GPT Image 2 sizing (quality knob only), Kling 4K and the Omni / Turbo / 2.6 tiers, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images, Smart Length, Gemini Omni Flash, exact inpaint masks (approximate ones work), and the upscalers. Prices are pass-through list rates for text and images; video carries a modest margin.
Which path should you pick? › 3. OpenRouter + fal.ai — pick this if you want aggregator simplicity at better video rates

Two keys instead of one, and the route table quietly picks the better door per model: OpenRouter keeps text, Marcel, and images (its native-menu fidelity wins there); fal takes over video — its Kling rates run noticeably cheaper — and adds GPT Image 2 sizing via its own presets. This is the setup we'd suggest to most people who don't want provider consoles: one evening of video work typically pays for the second key's two minutes of setup.

Keys you add later always take over their models automatically. Silent content refusals. An image edit returning finishReason: OTHER (newer builds: IMAGE_OTHER) is a content refusal, usually caused by an input image (a real person's name in facade text, a face, a logo), not the prompt.
