OpenAI takes an Inpaint mask as its native mask input. The mask steers where the change goes, but it doesn't lock the rest: GPT Image 2 and 2.5 redraw the whole image, so the area outside the mask comes back close to the original, not pixel-identical. We measured it on real runs (on a 2048² Flare edit, 0.1 % of the pixels far from the mask came back identical), and OpenAI's image guide says the same: "Masking with GPT Image is entirely prompt-based. The model uses the mask as guidance, but may not follow its exact shape with complete precision." When the rest must stay pixel-exact, stack the result over the original in a Layers node and mask it to the region you changed. Inputs are sent at multiples of 16. Since 2026-10-01 an edit's input image (and its mask) goes out center-cropped to the nearest multiple of 16 on both axes, at most 15 pixels per axis, as a lossless PNG, and the output size is derived from that: a 2048 × 1143 render is sent as 2048 × 1136 and comes back at 2048 × 1136. Before, GPT Image resampled the frame into its 16-multiple output and the whole picture crept by a few pixels (the "drift" on populate and relight passes). Nothing else is resampled. The output is the input's size. Since 2026-09-09 Brut always sends OpenAI an explicit output size: with a mask, the input image's own dimensions (so a 2K render comes back at 2K, nothing resampled); without one, aspect auto means the input's aspect at the size tier you picked (1K / 2K / 4K). Before that, OpenAI's own auto let the model choose the output size — a 2048² inpaint came back at 1254², and edits of a 3500×5000 render came back around 1000×1600, on GPT Image 2 too. Explicit sizing also makes the cost estimate honest: every run lands on a table cell.

Brut sends no temperature to the GPT-5-class planning models. Truncation is handled loudly: a finish_reason: length triggers one retry with more headroom, then a clear failure — never a silently cut-off plan.

Kling supports dual auth, and Brut accepts both: New style — an api-key-kling-… token, used as a plain Bearer token. Legacy — an AccessKey : SecretKey pair. Twelve image-to-video models (Kling 1.x through 3.0 Turbo). On the node you set duration, resolution, and — where the model supports it — audio and an end frame (Brut's engine-wide convention: the end frame is the second init image).

Default base is https://api-singapore.klingai.com; override with the BRUT_KLING_BASE environment variable for mainland China. Kling's own docs return HTTP 446 to automated fetchers, so some passthrough knobs (aspect_ratio, audio) are best confirmed by trying them — a wrong knob surfaces the provider's 4xx verbatim on the node.

The same Kling models, billed to your kling.ai subscription plan instead of API credit packs — measured at roughly 3× cheaper than the REST API, with no 30-day pack expiry. This is the recommended way to run Kling for steady studio work.
How it's authenticated (no key to paste)

There's no API key here. Auth is an OAuth session owned by Kling's official CLI — and setup is two buttons on the ⚙ Settings → Kling (subscription) card (or in the setup wizard): Install Kling CLI — one click. Brut fetches the official CLI (@klingai/cli-global, about 1 MB) straight from Kling's npm registry channel and runs it on the Node runtime that ships inside the Brut installer. Nothing else to install, no admin rights. Log in to Kling — your browser opens on kling.ai; sign in there. Tokens are stored by the CLI itself in ~/.kling/.credentials. Check login confirms the session any time, and Log out (shown while signed in) drops it — switch accounts by logging out, then logging back in with the other one. Finished generations stay on disk. The Kling (subscription) card: Install the CLI, Log in to Kling, and your plan balance once signed in If you run Brut from source instead of the installer, the classic route still works and takes precedence: `npm i -g @klingai/cli-global`, then `kling login` — a CLI already on your PATH is always used as-is. Brut talks to Kling through the CLI (an MCP client) and never keychains those tokens — the vault just reports a cli-oauth sentinel when the session file exists. The engine downloads the watermark-free master (result URLs expire in 24 h).

The subscription model ids differ from REST — kling-video-v2_5, …-v3_0, …-v3_0_omni, …-v3_0_turbo, …-v2_6, …-o1 — and cover both image-to-video and text-to-video. Reference images: o1 and 3.0 Omni take up to 6 extra references besides the start frame — the Image → Video node grows a references inlet when you pick them.

Only v2.5 currently carries a measured price (15 credits / 5s / 720p, ~3× cheaper than API list). Other tiers show no estimate until measured — Brut never invents a price it hasn't confirmed. Google's rules, applied on the node

Google's endpoint has rules of its own. Brut applies them before any call (checked on all three tiers, 2026-10-02): 1080p and 4K render at 8 s only. The Resolution and Duration selects grey the picks that cannot go together, in place, with the reason on hover, and a ⚠ line under the selects says what to change; your current pick is never swapped behind your back. 4K exists on Veo 3.1 and 3.1 Fast only (not on Lite); its estimate comes from Google's own price list ($0.60 and $0.30 per second, audio included) until a clip has run. On Film Shots, where the durations come from the plan, a 1080p pick snaps every clip to 8 s, the line under the select says so, and the itemized confirm lists the 8 s rows. Reference images need 8 s clips. With references wired, 4 s and 6 s grey out. Audio is always on. Google's own endpoint takes no audio switch on any 3.1 tier: every clip comes with sound and bills the audio rate, so the box shows ticked and greyed. A graph saved with the switch off is sent with audio, and the Activity panel says so. Through OpenRouter the switch still works, silent clips included. A request that still breaks a rule (an older graph, a hand-written plan) fails before the call, naming the fix: never a provider error for a combination the node could have refused. The Veo video prompt preset on Refine writes prompts in Veo's own film vocabulary; put exclusions in the node's negative-prompt field as plain nouns rather than in the prompt.

Veo submits a long-running operation and Brut polls it to completion, then downloads the clip. Field names have moved across preview releases, so Brut extracts the video URI tolerantly and reports parse issues loudly — including content-filter flags (raiMediaFiltered*). As a preview line, expect Google to occasionally shift a field name; Brut surfaces the raw error rather than hiding it.
Google's Gemini Omni Flash (gemini-omni-1.1-flash) is a fast natively-multimodal video model: picture and sound generated together, a clip in under a minute, about $1 per clip. Added 2026-08-28.
The key: it rides your Gemini key

Like Veo, Omni uses the same Google key as Gemini by default. If you've added a Gemini key, Omni just works; Brut reports the source as alias:gemini. Add a dedicated key in ⚙ Settings → Gemini Omni only to split the billing.

Image-to-video from a start frame, optionally with an end frame (the two-image interpolation), and text-to-video. 3 to 10 seconds, 16:9 or 9:16, output at 360p, 720p, 1080p or 4k. Note that 1080p and 4k are upscales of the 720p render, not a sharper generation; if you plan a Topaz pass anyway, generate at 720p. Reference images on the references inlet: extra images of a subject (a product, a character, a facade) the clip should stay faithful to. Name them in the prompt. Audio is always on. There is no switch; describe the sound you want, or say "no dialogue, no music, natural ambience only". Every clip carries Google's invisible SynthID watermark. No negative-prompt field exists on Omni: whatever you type in the node's negative prompt is folded into the prompt as "Avoid: …", which is Google's own advice. The Gemini Omni video prompt preset in Refine writes the flowing-prose prompt style Omni reads best.

Omni lives on Google's Interactions API, a different endpoint from both Gemini images and Veo. Brut submits the interaction in the background, polls it, then downloads the finished file through Google's Files API. The ledger row is priced from the token usage Google reports ($17.50 per million video tokens), so the spend readout shows the billed amount, not the estimate.
Pricing: flat per clip, so ask for 10 seconds

Google's page says "about $0.10 per second at 720p" (5,792 video tokens per second). What we measured on 2026-08-28 is that every clip is billed 57,920 video tokens — a 3-second 360p clip and an 8-second 720p clip cost exactly the same — which is the 10-second maximum × 5,792. So a generation is ≈ $1.01 whatever its length or resolution (360p/720p measured; 1080p/4k upscales not yet, the node shows $? there). The practical rule: ask for 10 seconds — the node defaults to it — and trim in the Sequence node if you want less. If Google's billing page shows you something different, tell us; the ledger keeps the raw token counts. Google keeps the interaction (your prompt, inputs and the clip) on its side for a while after it completes; that is what lets Omni edit its own earlier clips. Brut doesn't use that yet: editing and extending clips arrive with the Video → Video node after the September conference, together with the region note that matters for European users (Google doesn't allow editing or extending uploaded videos from the EEA, Switzerland or the UK; editing clips Omni generated itself is allowed).

Anthropic's Claude joins Brut as a planning model — text only. It generates no images or video; it's there to be your director: writing the concept, look and shot plan on the Director node, and powering the Refine node.

New on 28 September 2026, in Brut the day Anthropic released it. Sonnet 5.5 is Anthropic's newest Sonnet: faster and sharper than Sonnet 5, at the same price. Marcel's default brain. With an Anthropic key, Marcel's Auto brain is now Sonnet 5.5 (it was Sonnet 5). A brain you picked yourself in ⚙ Settings → Marcel stays picked. In every model picker: the Director, the crew agents, Text→Text, Refine and Marcel. It runs on your Anthropic key, or through OpenRouter at the same rates. Price: $2 in / $10 out per million tokens, the same as Sonnet 5. Marcel's long system context is cached, so after the first message of a session each turn costs cents. Reasoning goes from low to max (default high). Thinking off means no thinking before acting on this model, and works at low, medium or high effort only. Details under Reasoning dial & thinking switch. Marcel keeps talking while he works. Sonnet 5.5 (and Opus 5.5) write their notes between actions in a new form that stays hidden unless the app asks for it. Brut asks for it on every acting turn, so the notes appear in the chat as before. It also hands each step's reasoning back to the model unchanged, as Anthropic requires. Without that, Marcel went quiet mid-action and later apologised for notes you never saw.

New on 7 October 2026, in Brut the next morning. Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic's new small model: a tenth of Haiku 4.5's price, a 1M-token context, and the same two knobs as the big Claudes. The narrator's new default. With an Anthropic key, Marcel's Auto narrator lane (failure diagnoses, run commentary, recaps, the quiet taste passes) now runs on Haiku 5.5. A narrator you picked yourself stays picked. It is also in every text picker: the Director, the crew agents, Text→Text, Refine and Marcel's brain. Price: $0.10 in / $0.50 out per million tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. Over 100,000 tokens a prompt pays five times that ($0.50 / $2.50): the one current Claude priced by prompt length. Brut's estimates and ledger rows apply the higher rate when a call's prompt passes the line, which a long chat on Marcel's full knowledge can do; the narrator's few hundred tokens never do. Reasoning goes from low to max; thinking is adaptive by default and switches off cleanly (a plain off, unlike Sonnet 5.5's "no thinking before acting"). Runs on your Anthropic key, or through OpenRouter at the same base rates.
Create a key in the Anthropic Console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Anthropic (Claude). Brut validates it by listing models.

Anywhere Brut asks "which LLM should plan this?" — the Director (and the legacy crew agents), Text→Text and the Refine presets — you can pick Claude, Gemini or GPT. Claude reads your stills (multimodal, downscaled to fit the request cap; generation always uses full-resolution images) and returns the strict JSON plan the chain expects.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic's newest Sonnet, in Brut since its release day, 2026-09-28), Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5 (added 2026-08-23) and Opus 5.5 (launched 2026-09-22, in Brut since 2026-09-24) carry the knobs Brut exposes wherever these models run — the Text→Text node, the cinema agents, and Marcel's brain lane: Reasoning effort (low → max): how deeply the model reasons before answering. Deeper = better on hard treatments, more output tokens billed. Claude's own default is high on every model but Opus 5.5, whose default is medium: on 5.5, set the dial when you want the deep end. Thinking switch (Marcel's brain, ⚙ Settings): Claude Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 5 think adaptively by default, and those thinking tokens bill as output tokens — so if Marcel feels slow or a chat turn costs more than expected, switching thinking off is the lever: faster, cheaper, a little shallower. The switch needs your native Anthropic key (turns routed through an aggregator can't carry it — Brut refuses loudly rather than silently thinking anyway). Opus 5.5 has no switch: its thinking is always on (Anthropic rejects "off"), so the row reads not supported and the cost lever there is a low effort. On Sonnet 5.5, off means "no thinking before acting": Anthropic's lowest setting on that model still lets it write short progress notes between actions, and it works at low, medium or high effort only (with the dial at xhigh or max, Brut asks you to lower it or turn thinking back on). Haiku 5.5 carries both knobs too (thinking adaptive by default, a plain off). Haiku 4.5 supports neither (it was the narrator lane until Haiku 5.5 took over).

Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10 per million tokens in / out): Marcel's default brain since 2026-09-28 and the everyday planner, faster and sharper than Sonnet 5 at the same price. Sonnet 5 ($2 / $10): the previous Sonnet, still listed for graphs and lanes that picked it. Opus 5.5 ($4 / $20): the powerhouse brain, Opus-tier reasoning below Opus 5's price. Prompt-cache reads bill at 0.05× the input rate on this model, half the usual, so long Marcel sessions stay cheap. Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 ($5 / $25): still listed for graphs and lanes that picked them. Haiku 5.5 ($0.10 / $0.50 up to 100K tokens of prompt, $0.50 / $2.50 above): the narrator lane since 2026-10-08, and the cheapest Claude for Refine and Multi-Shot plans. Haiku 4.5 ($1 / $5): the previous narrator, still listed for lanes that picked it. List rates as pinned in Brut's catalog on 2026-10-08; every ledger row prices from the tokens the provider reports, never from a guess.

Truncation is handled loudly: a stop_reason: max_tokens triggers one retry with more headroom, then a clear failure — never a silently cut-off plan. Because Claude is text-only, it never enters the paid generation queue — it's a cheap planning brain, not a renderer. For available model ids and pricing, see Anthropic's console; Brut's catalog lists the ones it exposes.

Seedance (BytePlus ModelArk) is ByteDance's video family with native audio: a clip comes with sound in one pass. Brut carries Seedance 2.5 (the current flagship, added 2026-08-28), Seedance 2.0, and the 2.0 family's two cheaper tiers, Fast and Mini (added 2026-10-03).

Create a ModelArk key in the BytePlus console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Seedance (or set ARK_API_KEY). The same key serves Seedream images. Activate the model first. ModelArk models are switched on per account: open the console's Model activation page and activate each model you will run (Seedance 2.5, 2.0, and the Seedream models) before the first call. It is a one-time switch. Until then every request fails with "Your account … has not activated the model dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628"; Brut shows that message verbatim on the node. How BytePlus bills you. Everything is pay-as-you-go, and resource packs are optional: Credits (recommended): prepaid by card from Billing → Billing overview in the console, minimum USD 5 per top-up, they never expire, and the balance is a hard ceiling on spend. A balance of USD 30 unlocks the Seedance family (Seedream needs no minimum). Automatic billing: a bound card charged when consumption reaches a threshold (USD 50 by default) and on the 2nd of each month. No ceiling on BytePlus's side, so Brut's project budget caps are the ceiling. Resource packs are optional: one model each, 90 days, priced at the list rate, outside promotions. An activated model keeps running on the card or the credits after any pack is used up. A Savings Plan exists too; you do not need one. PayPal-only accounts cannot run pay-as-you-go ModelArk: add a card, or buy a pack.

Seedance 2.5 (dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628, first in the menu): Image-to-video from a start frame, or start + end frame, and text-to-video. 4 to 30 seconds in one clip, or smart length (the model picks). Long single takes are its headline. 480p, 720p, 1080p (1080p is 10-bit HEVC: it plays in VLC/mpv and modern browsers; older players may refuse it). Up to 30 reference images on the references inlet (a Reference Board plugs in). Address them in the prompt as @Image1, @Image2… in wiring order and say what each supplies ("@Image1 is the building, copy its materials exactly"). The clip's aspect ratio follows the start frame. Seedance 2.5 refuses a ratio on frame-to-video runs, so the node hides the aspect select and says so. Text-to-video keeps the full menu (16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4, 21:9, 1:1). Draft mode (on BytePlus's side since 2026-09-22, in Brut since 2026-09-24): a 480p draft take costs exactly what a 480p clip costs, and for seven days it can be re-rendered as the same shot at 1080p from its task id, billed like a 1080p clip. Explore at 480p, pay 1080p only for keepers. In Brut: the Draft take box on Image → Video (and Draft takes on Film Shots), then ⬆ Render final. Your own BytePlus key only. Native audio on by default (it costs nothing extra). Prompt grammar: integer-second beats (0-3s: …, 3-8s: …), () for music, <> for sound effects, {} for dialogue, "no BGM" / "no audio" when you want silence. The Seedance 2.5 video prompt preset in Refine writes this structure for you; Seedance 2.5 shot plan rewrites a whole cinema plan in it. Seedance 2.0 (dreamina-seedance-2-0-260128): 4 to 15 seconds (or smart length), up to 4K, first/last frame, reference images, and it accepts an explicit aspect ratio on frame-to-video runs. Still the choice when you need 4K straight out of the model. Its grammar is different (shot labels rather than timestamps, full-width audio symbols): use the Seedance 2.0 video prompt and Seedance 2.0 shot plan presets for it. Both generations stay in the menu; pick per job. Seedance 2.0 Fast (dreamina-seedance-2-0-fast-260128) and Seedance 2.0 Mini (dreamina-seedance-2-0-mini-260615) are the same family at a lower rate: 4 to 15 seconds (or smart length), 480p and 720p only, first and last frame, text-to-video, up to 9 reference images, native audio, the 2.0 prompt grammar (so the Seedance 2.0 video prompt preset). No draft mode: that is 2.5's. Mini is the cheapest video in Brut, about $0.18 for a 5-second 480p clip at list price; use it to test a move before paying for the 2.5 or 2.0 render. Both also run through OpenRouter. Watermark is always off. Video editing, extension and video/audio references exist on 2.5's API and come to Brut as a Video → Video node after the September conference. No BytePlus key? Both generations also run through an OpenRouter key, marked ⇄ runs via OpenRouter on the node. Seedance 2.5 there is 480p/720p only, 4 to 30 s, first and last frame, no reference images, no smart length and no draft mode, billed per video token at the same rate as BytePlus (the ledger records the exact billed amount). The 1080p tier, the 30-reference workflow and draft mode need your own BytePlus key.

Every clip comes with its last frame. Brut asks Seedance to return the clip's final frame as an image (at the clip's exact size, no watermark, not billed) and keeps it beside the clip. On Image → Video, ⏭ Last frame → Image In drops it on the canvas: wire it into the next clip's start frame to continue the shot. Because BytePlus made that frame, the people in it are accepted as a start frame (measured; see the faces gotcha below). A start frame and references can't travel together. Seedance refuses a request that carries both an exact first_frame and reference images. When you wire references into Image → Video, Brut switches to Seedance's keyframe reference mode, where the start (and end) frame are sent as references too. The framing is then approximate rather than pixel-exact and the clip's aspect is measured from the start frame. The node says so on its references line; wire no references to keep the exact first-frame behaviour. Photoreal faces are refused in reference images, generated or not. ModelArk's moderation blocks reference images or videos that look like they contain a real person, and it cannot tell an AI-generated face from a photograph (field-tested: a fully generated woman was refused as "may contain real person"). Only faces made by ModelArk's own models under your account, their preset digital characters, or authorized-person assets pass. Since 2026-10-02 Brut carries the first of those: people generated by Seedream 5.0 on your own key are trusted as Seedance start frames and references for 30 days, and the trust survives a resize or a re-export. The rule we measured: a Seedream picture made from text passes on Lite, Pro and Flash, and so does a frame of a Seedance clip; an edit (Image → Image) is refused like a picture from any other maker, on every Seedream model, and a crop of an accepted picture is refused too. The refusal message on the node names the refused picture (the start frame, reference 2) and this path. A populated archviz render from another model can trip this too; crop people out of the references, keep them in the start frame only, or do character swaps on Gemini Omni or Kling Omni, whose gates accept generated people. Three concurrent tasks per individual account. Film Shots sends five at once; the extra ones queue on BytePlus's side and finish a little later, nothing fails. Output URLs live 24 hours on their side; Brut downloads every clip as soon as it's done. A draft can be finalized for seven days, counted by BytePlus from the task's creation. Brut counts from the moment the draft landed, a few minutes later, so a click right at the edge can meet the provider's refusal; the node shows it verbatim. The final must ask for 1080p and the same model; Brut sends nothing else, because BytePlus refuses a re-sent prompt or frame "even if the values match".
Pricing, read this before you buy credits

Seedance's billing has two sharp edges (how to pay at all is under Get a key above): Credit packs are model-bound, and optional. A Seedance 2.5 pack does not cover 2.0 (or the fast/mini tiers), and vice versa. Buy the pack that matches the model you'll run, or stay pay-as-you-go on credits or your card. Rates are per token, and tokens depend on resolution and on whether the request contains video. Tokens ≈ width × height × 24 × seconds ÷ 1024. Brut's catalog turns BytePlus's list rates into per-second estimates: Seedance 2.5 ~ per second (16:9, no video input) 480p $0.10 720p $0.23 1080p $0.57 list, $0.41 through 17 September 2026 (BytePlus launch promo, applied automatically until that date) Seedance 2.0 ~ per second 480p $0.07 720p $0.15 1080p $0.37 4K $0.78 Seedance 2.0 Fast / Mini ~ per second (16:9, no video input, list price) Fast, 480p $0.056 Fast, 720p $0.12 Mini, 480p $0.035 Mini, 720p $0.076 BytePlus runs a discount on Fast and Mini for enterprise-verified accounts only (through 7 October 2026, capped). Brut cannot know your account's status, so the estimate and the ledger row show the list price; an enterprise account is billed less than Brut says. The node shows the estimate before you run, and Film Shots itemizes it per clip. The ledger row is priced from BytePlus's own token count (the usage the API returns), not from the estimate, so what you see in the spend readout is what you were billed. Failed generations cost nothing. A draft take bills like a 480p clip and its final like a 1080p clip: no discount on either, the saving is that you render 1080p only for the shots you keep, and the final is the same shot, not a new roll of the dice.

Seedream (BytePlus ModelArk) is ByteDance's image family. Brut carries the Seedream 5.0 trio since 2026-10-02: Pro, Flash and Lite, for text-to-image and image-to-image, on the same BytePlus key as Seedance. It is the cheapest photoreal tier in Brut, and the one BytePlus trusts for people that Seedance will animate.

Nothing new to paste. Seedream rides your Seedance key automatically: ⚙ Settings → Seedream reads uses your Seedance (BytePlus) key. Set a key there only to split Seedream's billing from Seedance's. Activate the models first. Like every ModelArk model, each one is switched on once per account: open the console's Model activation page (console.byteplus.com/ark) and activate Seedream 5.0 Pro, Seedream 5.0 Flash and Seedream 5.0 Lite. No resource pack is needed: activation is a one-time switch and the images bill pay-as-you-go on the account's credits or card (see Seedance, pricing). Until then a call fails with "has not activated the model", shown verbatim on the node. Lite comes with a free quota of 50 images.

Model Id Sizes Price per image Inputs Seedream 5.0 Pro dola-seedream-5-0-pro-260628 1K · 1.5K · 2K $0.045 at 1K and 1.5K, $0.09 at 2K; from the second input image $0.003 each up to 10 reference images Seedream 5.0 Flash dola-seedream-5-0-flash-260915 1K · 1.5K · 2K $0.018, any size up to 10 reference images Seedream 5.0 Lite seedream-5-0-lite-260128 2K · 3K · 4K $0.035, any size up to 14 reference images Pro is the quality tier (BytePlus's pick for "commercial visual production": precise editing, lifelike scenes). Flash is the same family at a third of the price, for exploration and high-volume passes. Lite is the older line with the biggest canvases and 50 free images. Speed, measured on 2026-10-02: Flash about 15 s for a 1K image, Pro about 30 s, Lite about 75 s at 2K. 1.5K bills like 1K and BytePlus calls it the better quality pick, so Pro and Flash default to it; Lite defaults to 2K. All three appear wherever an image model is picked: Text → Image, Image → Image, Inpaint, Compose, Multi-Shot, the Storyboard's keyframes, the Sketchpad's generation layers, the workflow cards' Model knobs. On Annotate & Correct, Pro and Flash are on the menu with their own way of reading the marks; Lite is not.

An explicit width × height, always. With a bare resolution preset, BytePlus lets the model decide the final size from the prompt (the same trap as OpenAI's size: auto). Brut asks for the exact pixels itself (a 16:9 image at 1K is 1424 × 800, at 2K 2816 × 1584). On an edit, aspect auto keeps the input's own proportions, and when the input already sits in the size you picked (a 2048 × 1143 render at 1.5K, say) it comes back at exactly its own dimensions. Pick a bigger or smaller size and the output moves to that size at the input's aspect, so the picture is resampled. Edits: Same as the picture. On Image → Image, Inpaint, Compose and Annotate & Correct, the Size menu opens with Same as the picture on all three Seedream models, and it is what the node takes when you switch it to Seedream. The result comes back at the input's pixel dimensions (the scene's, on Compose), so it lays over the original in a Layers or Compare node with nothing to scale. Each model's range sets the limit: Pro and Flash 0.9 to 4.6 MP, Lite 3.7 to 16.8 MP; below it the picture comes back at the model's smallest size, above it at its largest, the proportions kept. A node that already carries a picked size keeps it, and a stage hidden inside a workflow card keeps the size its card set: both have "Same as the picture" one pick away. PNG, lossless downstream (Layers, PSD export, Seedance frames), and watermark off: BytePlus stamps an "AI-generated" mark bottom right by default, Brut always turns it off. Your input files' exact bytes. Inputs travel as they are, never re-encoded or downscaled (that is what keeps BytePlus's trust signal on a Seedream original, below). The limits are checked before the call and fail loudly with the fix: 30 MB per image, 196 px² to 36 MP, both sides above 14 px, aspect between 1:16 and 16:1. Inpaint masks are guidance. Seedream has no native mask input, so on the Inpaint node the mask steers the edit, as on Gemini. Strong steering, never a pixel lock; stack the result over the original in Layers when the rest must stay exact. Output URLs live 24 hours on BytePlus's side; Brut downloads every image at once.
People for Seedance: the trusted path

ModelArk's moderation refuses Seedance start frames and references that look like they contain a real person, and it cannot tell a generated face from a photograph (see the Seedance gotchas). The exception BytePlus documents: since 2026-04-16, face-containing images generated by Seedream on your own account are trusted as Seedance 2.x input for 30 days (the doc names Lite text-to-image). Seedance's own clips and their frames are trusted the same way. We measured it with real requests and a clear face in frame, on Seedance 2.5, 2.0 Fast and 2.0 Mini, as a start frame and as a reference: The picture Seedance Seedream text-to-image, on Lite, Pro or Flash, the whole picture accepted One text-to-image character sheet (several views and expressions in one picture) accepted A frame of a Seedance clip (its last frame, or one taken from the middle) accepted Any Seedream edit (Image → Image), on Lite, Pro or Flash, even of a text-to-image picture refused A crop of an accepted picture refused The same portrait made by another maker refused A resize and a re-export (PNG, JPEG) keep the trust. A crop loses it, and so does anything that redraws the picture. An edit only gets through when no face is visible in it (people seen from behind, eyes hidden), which is the detector not firing, not trust: do not build on it. What this means in practice: One populated picture: write it as a Text → Image prompt on any Seedream model and wire the result, uncropped, into Image → Video. A character: the picture Seedance accepts is the one made from text. With the Character Lab, that is the design output when nothing is wired into character; its expression and turnaround sheets are edits of the design, so Seedance refuses them on every model. To give Seedance several views, write one text-to-image picture that is the whole sheet (full-body views in one row, expression close-ups in another) and wire that single picture as the reference. Continuing a shot: the last frame of a Seedance clip is accepted as the next clip's start frame. People added to an existing render (an edit): refused when a face shows. Keep faces out of view, or put the people in with the video prompt. When Seedance refuses a picture, the node's message says which wired picture it was (the start frame, reference 2) and repeats this rule. And before any run, the Image → Video node reads the ledger and shows which wired pictures carry the trust: see the trust line.

Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash can split one flat picture into a base (the scene with the elements lifted out and the gaps filled in) plus up to 16 layers with transparency, each with a name, a description and its place in the picture. In Brut: right-click any picture → Decompose into layers… (outputs, imports, board tiles, the magnifier), or Decompose result… under a Layers node's result. A small form asks for the model (Flash by default: the cheapest, and the one measured), the size and, if you want, what to separate ("the sky, the building, the trees in front, the people"). Leave that empty and the model picks the main elements itself. The price is shown before anything is spent. BytePlus bills every picture it returns, the base included: $0.018 each on Flash; on Pro $0.0225 each up to 2.61 MP and $0.045 above, each picture on its own pixels. How many layers come back is the model's call, so the dialog states the ceiling (16 layers and the base, 17 pictures: $0.31 on Flash) and the ledger row is priced from what actually came back. Measured on Flash: a 2752 × 1536 render split into a base and three layers (the sky, the building, the trees) in just under a minute for $0.072. The result lands as a new Sketchpad beside the picture: the base at the bottom, every layer above it in stacking order, scaled into its place and named by the model, and the original on top, hidden, one click on its eye away for a comparison. The node shows the recomposed picture at once. From there: move, scale, hide or mask a layer, paint between them, add a generation layer, or Export PSD and carry on in Photoshop. Right-click a render, Decompose into layers: the price, then a Sketchpad with the pergola, the bench, the building and each tree as its own layer The details: Size. Same as the picture (the default) brings the base back at the picture's own dimensions when it sits between 0.9 and 4.6 MP, so the stack lines up with the original pixel for pixel; a smaller picture comes back at 1K, a larger one at 2K. With this setting each layer also comes back at exactly its size in the picture, so nothing is rescaled. Or pick 1K, 1.5K or 2K yourself: the layers then come back near that resolution, usually larger than their place in the picture (detail to spare if you scale one up), and Brut scales them into place. One picture in, from 512 × 512 px to 36 MP, up to 30 MB. PNG and JPEG travel as they are; any other format (WEBP, TIFF) is converted to PNG on the way, losslessly. The model lifts each element out whole. Trees that stood behind a hedge can come back with their full trunks, which then show in front of the base. The words you give it steer what comes back; and in the Sketchpad a layer mask hides the part that should stay behind (select the layer, add a mask, paint black over the trunks). All or nothing. If one layer fails on BytePlus's side the whole call fails, and the message is shown as it came. Nothing lands on the canvas. Your own BytePlus key. The ability is not sold through OpenRouter: on a seat without the key the menu item stays in place, greyed, and says why. Every file is kept in the project's outputs, named after the run (…_sketch-12-layers_seedream_SR5F_…, then -2, -3 in stacking order). Find in ledger on the Sketchpad's preview, or on any of the files, shows the run with its cost.

Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash read positions written into the prompt: a point or a rectangle, as numbers between 0 and 999 across the picture. The Annotate & Correct node uses exactly that. Draw your marks as usual, pick Seedream on the node, run: each mark lands where you drew it, and nothing of the markup shows in the result. An arrow or a point marks a spot (for the arrow, its tip). A box, circle, lasso or polygon marks its bounding box. A mark's reference image and its color chip travel with that mark. Size: Same as the picture is the default on this node for Seedream: the result comes back at the picture's own dimensions (between 0.9 and 4.6 MP; a smaller picture comes back at 1K, a larger one at 2K), so the result and the original stack at the same size in a Layers node. Pick 1K, 1.5K or 2K to resample instead. The same size is not the same pixels: the model redraws the frame, and a result can sit a few pixels off its original (3 to 6 px on a 2752 × 1536 scene we measured). 🗇 Reconcile with input lays the result back over the original and keeps only the edits: everything else is the original's own pixels (how it works). When a box holds several things, name the one you mean in the note: the model gets the rectangle, not your outline. Five marks on a render, one of each kind, Seedream Flash on the node: each edit lands at its mark, for under two cents Measured on a 2048 × 1143 interior with five marks, one of each kind: both models applied all five at their marks and returned 2048 × 1143; Flash in 21 s for $0.018, Pro in 41 s for $0.045 (Pro matched the asked RAL green more closely). A second run placed an armchair from a reference image inside a box, turned the way the note asked, on both. The same marks through the drawn-copy route on Nano Banana 2 were all applied too, with two of them placed loosely. The table is on the [Annotate & Correct](/docs/nodes/image-generation.html#seedream-on-this-node) page.

The node shows the per-image price before the run (the output price: $0.045 / $0.018 / $0.035, Pro 2K $0.09). The ledger row is priced from what came back: the actual output pixels decide the tier (1K and 1.5K bill the same; above 2.61 MP is the 2K rate), and Pro's input-image surcharge is added from the count BytePlus reports ($0.003 per input after the first). Pinned on the first live runs (2026-10-02): every requested size came back exactly, and the usage block carries the token count (width × height ÷ 256) and the input count the ledger math uses. A moderation refusal is not billed and the node says so. A decomposition bills per picture returned (the base and each layer), at its own rate: $0.018 on Flash, $0.0225 or $0.045 on Pro. The price dialog states the ceiling, the ledger the real amount. No BytePlus key? All three also run through an OpenRouter key, marked ⇄ runs via OpenRouter on the node, with OpenRouter's size menu (1K / 2K for Pro and Flash, 2K / 4K for Lite; no 1.5K or 3K there) at OpenRouter's listed pass-through prices. The ledger records the exact billed amount of every routed job.

Lite's smallest output is 2K (its pixel floor is 3.7 MP); Pro and Flash render between 0.9 and 4.6 MP. The size menus follow each model. Why Pro and Flash stop at 2K. It is BytePlus's limit, not Brut's: those two models render at most 4.62 MP, which is a 2K picture (2816 × 1584 at 16:9). 3K and 4K exist on Lite only. For a 4K Seedream picture, use Lite on Text → Image, Image → Image, Inpaint or Compose; for a 4K result from a Pro or Flash edit, add an Upscale Image node after it. BytePlus recommends prompts under about 600 English words: longer prompts lose details rather than gain them. Sequential sets (Lite, up to 15 related images in one call) and transparent-background edits exist on the API and are planned for Brut. Layer decomposition and coordinate-addressed editing are in: see Decompose into layers and Annotate & Correct. You can also type the coordinate tags yourself in any Image → Image prompt on Pro or Flash (<point>520 460</point>, <bbox>120 180 640 760</bbox>, 0 to 999 from the top-left corner, the picture named "Image 1"): Brut passes the prompt as written. The Annotate node exists so you never have to.

Black Forest Labs makes the FLUX models. Brut calls their own API with your key, for two things: FLUX 3 Image, their flagship image model, in every image menu (Text → Image, Image → Image, Compose, Inpaint, Multi-Shot, the Storyboard's keyframes, the Sketchpad's generation layers). FLUX Outpaint, their outpainting tool, as a painter in Conform's extend. It is the one painter in Brut that holds your picture in place and generates only what the frame adds.

Create an account on the Black Forest Labs dashboard, add credits, make an API key and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Black Forest Labs (or set BFL_API_KEY). Billing is prepaid credits: 1 credit is $0.01, and a call on an empty balance answers "not enough credits". There is no subscription. Every answer says what the call cost, and that number is what Brut writes on the ledger row. No key? FLUX 3 Image also runs through OpenRouter on an OpenRouter key (the node says "⇄ via OpenRouter"). FLUX Outpaint is on Black Forest Labs' own API only: no aggregator carries it.

Sizes 768, 1K, 1.5K, 2K, 4K. These are pixel budgets, the same at every ratio: about 0.6, 1, 2.4, 4 and 17 megapixels (at 9:16: 576 × 1024, 768 × 1360, 1152 × 2048, 1536 × 2736, 3072 × 5456). Ratios Every ratio on Brut's menu, plus auto on an edit: the output keeps the first picture's framing. Pictures in Up to 10 per request, from 256 px a side to 16 megapixels each. Above 4 megapixels Black Forest Labs scales a reference down to 4 before it works on it. Price Per image, by size: $0.041 (768), $0.048 (1K), $0.07 (1.5K), $0.10 (2K), $0.607 (4K). Reference pictures and the prompt cost nothing extra; a refused request is not charged. Things worth knowing: It can look things up. By default FLUX 3 searches the web before it draws, which is how it gets a real building or a real product right. Brut leaves that on, except when Conform uses FLUX 3 to extend a picture (there is nothing to look up). It has no mask input. On the Inpaint node the mask steers the edit, as on Gemini. Like every mask in Brut it is guidance: the model redraws the frame. It is an edit model, not a fill model. Asked to extend a picture, it sometimes keeps your picture exactly where it was and sometimes recomposes the room. For an extension where the original must not move, use FLUX Outpaint. 4K is priced six times 2K. "Same as the picture" on a large frame lands on 4K; the frame editor shows the price before you paint, and 2K is one pick away.

A tool, not a model you prompt: it takes a picture, the size of the frame around it and where the picture sits in that frame, and paints the rest. It appears in one place, the painter menu of Conform's ✂ frame editor, when the method is extend, and it is the painter Conform starts on once your key is in. Your picture is held. Where the frame covers the picture, the output is the picture; the tool generates only the added part. That is the difference with every image model on the same menu, which redraw the whole frame. 4 megapixels at most. The tool's frame cannot exceed 4,194,304 pixels. A larger frame is painted smaller: a 2048 × 3641 frame comes back at 1520 × 2704 (the tool works in multiples of 16 pixels, so a frame can also lose a few pixels at its edges). Brut delivers that picture as it is and never scales it back up; Upscale Image is the way to more pixels. The frame editor says so under the picture before you paint. A size menu to paint smaller on purpose. Up to 4 MP is the default; up to 2 MP and up to 1 MP lower the limit, and the price with it. No prompt needed. The tool reads the picture and continues it. The still's optional note ("more lawn", "no new buildings") is passed along as a hint; the tool may or may not follow it. High or Fast. High (the default) gives the best continuation of the picture. Fast answers in seconds for about a sixth of the price; your picture is held just as well, but the painted part is rougher: on an interior, a grittier floor and a wall that stops at the seam where High carries it on. Fast suits a first look, and scenes that extend easily (sky, lawn, water, a plain background). Price. Black Forest Labs publishes no rate for this tool. Measured through Brut, counted on the whole frame, your picture included: High, $0.10 per megapixel ($0.10 at 1 MP, $0.20 at 2 MP, $0.40 at 4 MP); Fast, about $0.05 ($0.045 at 1 MP, $0.051 at 2 MP, $0.063 at 4 MP). The frame editor shows the price for your frame, size and mode before the paint; the ledger row carries the billed amount after it.

Up to 24 requests run at once on one account. Results are downloaded to your project the moment they are ready: the link Black Forest Labs returns lasts minutes. Their moderation can stop a request (the prompt or a picture) or a result. The node shows which, with their reason; a moderated call is not charged.

Calls go from your machine to api.bfl.ai with your key, and nowhere else. With web lookup on, FLUX 3 itself sends search queries drawn from your prompt: that happens inside Black Forest Labs' service.

Magnific is the reference AI image upscaler. Brut integrates its two upscaling endpoints — Upscaler Creative and Upscaler Precision V2 — in the Upscale Image node. Brut deliberately uses only the upscalers, not Magnific's other generation endpoints.

Generate an API key on your Magnific dashboard (API Keys page) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Magnific (or set MAGNIFIC_API_KEY). You do not need the webhook secret: Brut runs on your machine and polls Magnific for results directly — no webhooks, no third-party relay, nothing in the call path but you and Magnific.

The API bills credits from your Magnific subscription's allocation (for example, Premium+ includes 600K credits per year), consumed by output pixel area. Two things worth knowing: A credit's dollar value depends on your tier, so Brut doesn't pretend to convert: the ≈$ figure on the node is Magnific's own doc-derived pay-as-you-go equivalent — a rough ceiling, not what your plan actually charges you. On a yearly plan, your effective cost is simply your plan price spread over your usage; at studio volume upscales barely dent the allocation (a few hundred credits each against hundreds of thousands per year). "Unlimited" plans are unlimited in the web app only — API calls always consume credits. Brut would happily show your credit balance and per-run points instead — but Magnific's API exposes neither on individual plans (the analytics endpoints are reserved for team tiers, and task responses carry no credit field). If Magnific ships a balance endpoint, Brut will pick it up. Until then: your Magnific dashboard is the billing truth.

Brut sends the original file bytes — never a re-encode, never a downscale. If an image exceeds Creative's 25.3M-pixel input cap, the run fails with a clear message instead of quietly shrinking your work (use Precision V2, or crop deliberately). Upscales are async: they survive an engine restart and reattach, like video jobs — money spent is never output lost. Provider errors are surfaced verbatim on the node.

Topaz Labs powers the precision side of the Upscale Image node — the Gigapixel-class faithful upscalers (including a model tuned for renders and CGI) and the Wonder-class generative ones — plus the Upscale Video node (Proteus / Rhea / Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend). One key covers both. There are two ways to run Topaz video upscales in Brut: Topaz Labs (cloud) — the API below. Credits per job, works on any machine. Topaz Video AI (local) — if you own the Topaz Video desktop app and a capable GPU, Brut drives the app's own engine on your machine instead. No key, no credits, no cost per run — and the clip never leaves your computer. See local install below.
Create an API key on the Topaz developer portal and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Topaz Labs (or set TOPAZ_API_KEY).

Model Class When Gigapixel Standard 2 precision the everyday default Gigapixel High Fidelity 2 precision maximum source preservation Gigapixel Art & CGI precision archviz renders, illustrations, game assets Gigapixel Low Resolution 2 precision tiny sources, thumbnails Redefine generative photoreal invented detail, prompt + creativity dial Standard MAX generative true-to-input generative restoration Recover 3 generative damaged / heavily compressed sources Generative models cap input around 24–256 MP and cost more per pixel; the node fails loudly if your input × scale exceeds a model's cap — it never downscales your work silently.

Topaz bills credits by output megapixel: the standard class covers ~24 MP per credit, the generative class ~4 MP per credit, minimum one credit per job. Credits come from one-off packs or a subscription's monthly allowance — the per-credit price depends on how you buy (packs run roughly $0.195 down to $0.158 per credit; subscriptions less). Brut shows a pre-run estimate in credits (with an approximate $ at a representative rate), the node displays your live credit balance, and the spend ledger records the actual credits the API reports for each job. Your Topaz account page is the billing truth. Credits are the billing truth: the live balance on the card and the quantized estimate on the node ## Behavior notes Async like every upscaler: jobs survive an engine restart and reattach — money spent is never output lost. Results are downloaded to your project immediately (Topaz keeps files 7 days, links 1 hour — Brut never relies on either). Provider errors surface verbatim on the node; "not enough credits" says exactly that.

If Topaz Video (or the older Topaz Video AI) is installed and licensed on your machine, the Upscale Video node offers a second provider: Topaz Video AI (local). It runs the same models — Proteus, Rhea, Gaia CG — through the app's own engine on your GPU. No key and no account — Brut auto-detects the install (⚙ Settings shows "installed · free"); the app's own sign-in covers command-line use. If you install it mid-session, hit Check install. Free — no credits, no confirm dialog; the ledger records the run at $0. Private — the clip is processed entirely on your machine; nothing is uploaded. Missing model weights download automatically on first use (a one-time pause per model). Output is HEVC (H.265) with the clip's audio kept, like the cloud path. One run at a time — a second local upscale queues behind the first (one GPU). Local jobs don't survive an engine restart (nothing was billed, just re-run). The non-standard install location can be pointed at with BRUT_TVAI_DIR (the folder holding Topaz's ffmpeg.exe) and BRUT_TVAI_MODEL_DIR (its models folder).

fal.ai is an aggregator — a usage-billed API that resells many generation models under one key. Brut uses it as a route, not a provider in its own right: it never adds a single model to the menu, it just serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key for them. If you keep exactly one key on this machine, a fal.ai key is the widest single door: it can serve the Nano Banana image family, GPT Image 2, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, and Veo 3.1 — each visibly marked ⇄ runs via fal.ai on the node whenever the route is active.

Create a key on the fal.ai dashboard (it's an id:secret string) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → fal.ai (or set FAL_KEY). fal has no free generation tier — add billing to the fal account before the first call, or the first run answers with a provider error (shown verbatim, as always).

Your direct key always wins. The moment you add a native key (Gemini, Kling, BytePlus, …), that model leaves the fal route and bills direct — usually cheaper. Routing is always visible. The node chip, the paid-run confirm, and the spend ledger all say "via fal.ai". Nothing routes silently. Honest prices only. Estimates for routed runs use fal's own list prices where pinned, and show none at all otherwise — never the native provider's numbers. Image routes are pinned from fal's model cards and cross-checked against real dashboard charges (Nano Banana $0.0398 — essentially the native rate; Nano Banana 2 $0.06–$0.16 by size; Pro $0.15/$0.30 at 4K; GPT Image 2 per size × quality, e.g. square_hd high $0.211, square low $0.0053 measured). Expect a margin over the direct API elsewhere (Seedance via fal is roughly 2× the native BytePlus rate; video rates unpinned).
What the routes can and can't do

A route carries exactly the knobs fal's endpoint declares — anything else fails loudly instead of being quietly dropped. Current limits worth knowing: Veo via fal takes no end frame — unwire it or add your Gemini/Veo key. Inpaint masks route APPROXIMATELY on the Nano Banana models — the same convention as Gemini native (the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee; verified live). GPT Image 2 masks don't route: inpainting on GPT Image needs your OpenAI key. GPT Image 2 uses fal's own size presets (square, landscape 4:3/16:9, portrait, auto) — the node's Size menu shows exactly those instead of Brut's aspect + 1K/2K/4K pair. No silent mapping: the menu is the contract. Nano Banana (original) renders 1K only via fal; pick 2K/4K models or add your Gemini key. Kling 3.0's 4K master tier isn't on fal — std/pro only. Audio on video models is always sent explicitly (fal defaults it ON and bills extra — Brut keeps your node toggle authoritative). Generations behave like every other async provider: downloaded to your project's disk, journaled, restart-safe, priced in the ledger.

Higgsfield is an aggregator with a twist: it's billed by subscription plan credits, not an API key — which makes it the door into Brut for people who hold a higgsfield.ai plan and nothing else. Brut uses it as a route: it never adds a model to the menu, it serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key for them, always visibly marked ⇄ runs via Higgsfield on the node. Current mirror set (verified against the official tool's own model catalog): Images — Nano Banana (image→image), Nano Banana 2 (text/image→image), Nano Banana 2 Lite (text→image, 1K), Nano Banana Pro (text/image→image, up to 4K), GPT Image 2 (text/image→image, sizes as Higgsfield's 1k/2k/4k resolutions). Video — Kling v3 (with end frames), Kling v3 Turbo, Kling v2.6, Veo 3.1, Veo 3.1 Fast, Veo 3.1 Lite (with end frames, 8-second clips), Seedance 2.0 — including the Kling (subscription) menu entries, so a seat without the Kling sign-in falls back here instead of dead-ending. Where Higgsfield lacks a knob the native API has, the node hides it and says so in the price note — the common ones: no inpaint masks, no end frame on Kling 2.6 / v3 Turbo / Veo 3.1 (non-Lite), and no audio switch on Veo 3.1 (clips come with audio).

Higgsfield has no API key. Auth is a browser sign-in owned by Higgsfield's official command-line tool, which Brut manages for you. In ⚙ Settings → Higgsfield (subscription) (or the setup wizard): Install Higgsfield CLI — Brut fetches the official tool from Higgsfield's own GitHub release (≈19 MB, one time, integrity-checked). Nothing else is needed — the tool is self-contained. Log in to Higgsfield — your browser opens on higgsfield.ai; sign in with your normal account. The session is stored by Higgsfield's tool on your machine — Brut never sees or stores the credential. That's it: routed models light up the moment the sign-in lands. A Log out button appears while you're signed in — use it to switch accounts (finished generations stay on disk). Higgsfield's own platform carries many more models (Kling, WAN, Sora 2, Veo, Flux, Seedream…). Brut adds a route only after verifying each one's real API contract against the official tool — the list here grows as they're pinned, never speculatively.

Generations bill your plan's credits, exactly as if you'd used higgsfield.ai directly. Brut adds nothing and shows no invented USD estimates — credit rates aren't pinned yet, so routed runs show no price rather than a made-up one. The ledger still records every run. Your direct key always wins: add a Gemini or BytePlus key later and those models switch back to direct billing automatically. Higgsfield resells other providers' models under its own margin — if you generate a lot, a direct API key is usually cheaper. The subscription route is about simplicity, not price.

A routed run carries exactly the knobs the route declares — anything else fails loudly instead of being silently dropped (Inpaint masks, for example, don't route). Audio on video models always follows your node toggle — never Higgsfield's default. Provider-side tasks may not be cancellable: cancelling in Brut stops the polling, but plan credits may still be spent. Outputs are downloaded to your project's disk like every provider — restart-safe, journaled, in the ledger.

Replicate is the third aggregator route in Brut — a plain API-token, pay-per-use service that resells official builds of many models. Like every route, it never adds a model to the menu: it serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key (and no earlier route credential — fal.ai and Higgsfield are checked first), always visibly marked ⇄ runs via Replicate on the node. Current mirror set: Nano Banana Pro & 2 (text→image and image→image), GPT Image 2 (text→image and image→image), Kling 3.0 Omni, Veo 3.1 & 3.1 Fast (image→video and text→video), Seedance 2.0 (image→video and text→video).

Create a token at replicate.com/account/api-tokens (r8_…) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Replicate (or set REPLICATE_API_TOKEN). Billing must be enabled on the Replicate account before the first run — errors come back verbatim, as always.

Your direct key always wins, and fal.ai / Higgsfield credentials outrank Replicate when present (catalog order). Replicate is the redundancy door. Routing is always visible — node chip, run confirm, spend ledger. No invented prices: image routes carry Replicate's own billing-table rates (Nano Banana 2 $0.067 · Pro $0.15/$0.30 at 4K · GPT Image 2 $0.012/$0.047/$0.128 by quality); video rates aren't pinned yet, so those runs show no estimate rather than a wrong one. The ledger records every run.
What this route can do that fal's can't

Veo end frames work (last_frame is a real input on Replicate's Veo 3.1). Seedance text→video is available. GPT Image 2 sizes ride Replicate's aspect menu — ratios plus explicit sizes like 2048x1152 up to 3840x2160; the node's Aspect select shows exactly that menu (the entries above 2560x1440 are marked experimental by the schema). Reference images ride on Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0, and Kling 3.0 Omni.
And its own limits (all fail loud, never silent)

Seedance tops out at 720p on Replicate — 1080p/4K need your BytePlus key. Smart Length isn't available either. Nano Banana 2 has no size knob — 1K only; pick Nano Banana Pro for 2K/4K. Kling 4K master tier doesn't exist on Replicate (std/pro only), and the Kling route is the Omni model. Inpaint masks route approximately on the Nano Banana models (the Gemini convention: the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee). GPT Image 2 masks don't route: inpainting on GPT Image needs your OpenAI key. Audio always follows your node toggle, never Replicate's default. Large input images (multi-MB keyframes) are uploaded through Replicate's Files API automatically; outputs are downloaded to your project's disk immediately — restart-safe, journaled, in the ledger.

OpenRouter is the one aggregator key that can hold almost the whole of Brut: every text model (planning and Marcel — chat, ambient narration, acting), the full Nano Banana image family (incl. Nano Banana 2 Lite, the starter graph's model), GPT Image 2, GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst, the Seedream 5.0 trio (Pro / Flash / Lite at 1K / 2K, Lite 2K / 4K, since 2026-10-02), and the video models — Kling 3.0 and O1, Veo 3.1 / Fast / Lite, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5. Outside it: the upscalers (they aren't resold anywhere, by design), Gemini Omni Flash and the other Kling tiers (3.0 Omni / Turbo / 2.6 / 2.5 and older), which OpenRouter doesn't carry. Like every route, it adds no models to the menu and is always visible: routed nodes show ⇄ runs via OpenRouter, and Marcel's composer says so too. If you want the simplest possible seat: one OpenRouter key is a working studio. Native keys added later always take their models back automatically, usually at slightly better prices.

Every text model in Brut's catalog also runs here, at pass-through provider list rates — the same per-token prices as the native APIs (OpenRouter's revenue is a ~5.5% fee when you buy credits, not a token markup). Vision-grounded planning works, the GPT reasoning dial rides along (Marcel's tools included: OpenRouter bridges to OpenAI's Responses API, so the tools need none rule of the native chat wire does not apply here), and Anthropic prompt caching passes through — Marcel's long system context caches exactly as on a native Anthropic key (write premiums and 0.1× reads verified live), so routed conversations cost the same as native ones. Every model Brut adds gets its OpenRouter route when OpenRouter serves it (GPT-6 Sol and Luna joined the same day they entered the catalog): the route is how a seat without provider keys reaches the whole catalog with one key.

The Nano Banana family runs with Brut's own menus — the real 512/1K/2K/4K sizes and the full aspect list, unlike fal's preset system — which is why OpenRouter sits first in those models' route order. Approximate inpaint masks work (the Gemini convention, verified live). Billing is pass-through: on 28 September 2026 we ran every routed image model through Brut and each one billed the same as on the maker's own key, to the tenth of a cent. Nano Banana Pro cost $0.13 at 1K or 2K and $0.24 at 4K; Nano Banana 2 cost $0.07 / $0.10 / $0.15 at 1K / 2K / 4K; Lite $0.034 and the original Nano Banana $0.039. So the estimate before a run is the real price, and every image job records its exact billed amount on the ledger. Two OpenRouter-specific limits worth knowing: Requests cap at ~52 MB, and a full-resolution PNG render can eat that alone once base64-encoded. When an image stack wouldn't fit, Brut transcodes the largest PNG inputs to full-resolution JPEG (q95) for that request only — never downscaled, never touching your files, logged in the engine console. If even that can't fit, the run fails loudly; export the source smaller or use a native key. Heavy 4K image jobs can be slow. OpenRouter's image endpoint is synchronous, and its queue sometimes stalls on large 4K multi-image jobs (measured in the field: a 4K edit that takes ~55 s on a native Gemini key can exceed Brut's 570 s route timeout entirely — that's on their end, not yours). If you hit the timeout: retry, pick a smaller size, or use the native key — which is the first-class lane anyway and takes over automatically the moment it's configured. The one exception is GPT Image, which OpenRouter renders at about 1K only: there's no size knob, so 2K and 4K need your OpenAI key. The aspect ratio and the quality do come through, on GPT Image 2 and on the GPT Image 2.5 pair alike: 2.5 keeps its full low to max quality menu, and image-to-image with aspect auto follows your input's shape. Masks don't: inpainting on GPT Image needs the OpenAI key. Measured on 28 September 2026: a 1:1 image costs $0.006 at low and $0.053 at high on 2.5 (the same on Flare and Sunburst), and 16:9 costs less ($0.004 at low). For GPT Image 2, fal and Replicate still outrank OpenRouter because they can size the image.
Video — the whole set, with billing truth

Kling 3.0 (std/pro) and Kling O1 (5 or 10 s, 720p, $0.112/s — the REST and subscription O1 entries both route here), Veo 3.1 / Fast / Lite (OpenRouter is the first route Lite has ever had), Seedance 2.0 and Seedance 2.5 (480p/720p only, 4–30 s, first + last frame, no reference images there — the 30-reference and 1080p features need the BytePlus key) — image-to-video with end frames, text-to-video, reference images where the listing declares them.
