Create a key at openrouter.ai/keys (sk-or-…), buy a few dollars of credits, and paste it into ⚙ Settings → OpenRouter (or set OPENROUTER_API_KEY).

Your native key always wins. Add a Gemini/OpenAI/Kling/… key later and those models bill direct again automatically. A fal.ai key can also run text (fal resells the same router) — but fal's text lane takes no images and no reasoning dial, so OpenRouter outranks it when both keys exist. Marcel routes here and only here: his lanes stream, and OpenRouter is the one aggregator whose wire supports Brut's streaming + tool-call + prompt-cache contract. Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance's Smart Length, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images aren't on OpenRouter; Kling O1 takes only 5 or 10 s there. For video, fal outranks OpenRouter when both keys exist (fal's Kling rates run cheaper). Missing knobs always fail loud, never silently. Every routed call — text, image, or video — lands in the spend ledger with provider-reported figures (token counts, cache activity, billed cost), marked "via openrouter".

Brut's most ambitious workflow: turn a handful of stills into a finished, cut sequence — planned by a crew of AI agents, shot on the video provider of your choice, and assembled locally with ffmpeg, for exactly the bill it showed you. Stills → a crew that plans the film → a storyboard you edit → clips shot behind a confirm gate → a sequence cut on your machine. You stay in control at every step.

Conform → Reference Board → Director (plan + proof sheet) → Storyboard (keyframes) → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview Every arrow is a wire. The Director passes a plan document (JSON on a text wire); the boards are where you review and curate. Don't build this by hand the first time: the whole chain ships as the Stills → Film card (the library's From Brut shelf, or the home's Workflows row): one composite whose knobs are the Director's dials (brief, style, shots, runtime, people, audio), the film aspect and the clips' Quality (720p, 1080p or 4k). The models are pinned to the field-proven set: GPT 5.6 Terra plans, GPT Image 2.5 Flare renders the proof sheet and the keyframes (xhigh, 2K), Kling 3.0 on your kling.ai plan shoots the clips with audio; open (⤢) the card to change any of them. Wire your stills in, set the knobs, run: the Director plans, its proof sheet renders right after and opens for your call (take it, a new take, or ✗ frames and reinvent them; stop, and nothing downstream runs), then the keyframe batch and the Film Shots table still ask before any spend. The card's 📖 Plan opens the Director's document to read, edit and annotate, its 🎬 Proof sheet reopens the sheet any time; open the card to judge the keyframes and the clips on their boards. Finish in 4K is the next card it offers. Let's walk what it does. The Stills → Film card: the whole chain from stills to the cut, one composite with its dials on the face ## 1 · Prepare the stills Start from your renders — an Image In node (or a Multi-Shot contact sheet you've curated). Run them through Conform to a single aspect ratio (video wants consistency), cropping each to keep the right part of the frame. Wire the conformed stills into a Reference Board. This makes the pool visible and numbered — and the tile number is the still number the crew will refer to. Reorder to taste; the plan refers to the stills by these numbers.

One Director node. It writes the concept, the look and the shot plan together, and the film comes out varied: an arc across the shots, lenses and framing changing shot to shot, no still used twice in a row. Pick a Brief and a Style, set shots and runtime, choose how much human presence you want, and wire it straight into the Storyboard. Every clip also gets a one-line ambient sound note for video models that produce audio. Before anything spends on keyframes, the Director's 🎬 proof sheet renders right after the plan, in the same run: one cheap image of the whole film as a numbered contact sheet, all frames in one grade. The run then stops on it and asks for your call. Select the frames that don't inspire you and ✎ Reinvent rewrites only those clips (the others stay exactly as they were) and re-renders the sheet for cents; ↻ New take re-rolls the same plan; Take this sheet lets the run go on (a later run with the same sheet never asks again); Stop runs nothing downstream. 📌 pin the sheet you validate to keep it through plan edits. The sheet you take guides every keyframe: what you approved is what gets produced. Run the Director: concept, look and the executable shot plan land in one call; the proof sheet renders the whole film for cents Pick the Director's LLM — **Gemini, GPT or Claude** — on your own key. The plan is **editable text**: tweak a line and it flows downstream. Don't read the raw JSON — the node's **📖 Review** opens the plan as an actual document: edit it in place for free, or leave **💬 margin notes** and let **Revise** apply them ([details](/docs/nodes/cinema-crew.html)). The four-agent crew (Scenarist / Artistic Director / DoP / Script Supervisor) is legacy since 1.1.1: the Director plans better films, so the crew nodes are hidden from the node browser. Graphs that already use them keep loading and running exactly as before — details.
2 · The Director plans the film › Invented shots — the flourish

Your stills define the project's identity, not the shot list. The Director invents most compositions — a detail close-up, a reveal, subtle human presence, the pull-back ending — each anchored on the stills that carry its materials, with a written keyframe prompt already styled to the film's look. The rule never loosens, it moves one level: one clip = one keyframe. An invented shot's start frame is generated from its anchor stills and the proof sheet you took, at the film's aspect, before any video runs. An invented shot is never quietly sent as text-to-video — without an approved keyframe it simply refuses to roll. Want the full reel behavior? The Director's "Invent every shot" switch makes the stills references only — no shot animates one directly, every start frame is generated. Off, the brief decides shot by shot.

The Storyboard turns the plan into shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, and ✕ mutes a card (greyed, kept, ↺ to bring it back) rather than deleting it. Change a line here and only that shot re-renders. It emits concrete image paths, so the next node just needs the plan wire. The plan you see always matches the board's tiles. An anchor that points at a still the board doesn't have fails loudly on its card, never silently, and 📖 Review on the Director lets you rewrite a shot's anchors by hand. Invented shots arrive frameless. Each shows its keyframe prompt and a 🎨 Generate keyframe button — pick the image model, resolution and (on GPT Image) quality once at the top of the board (the pending count and per-frame price sit next to it and follow your picks; keyframes are cents, clips are dollars). Generated keyframes cache on their prompt + anchors (an unchanged card never re-pays), ↻ re-rolls a fresh take, 📌 pins one against later prompt edits, 🕘 opens the card's history — every take it ever generated, from the project ledger — so a re-roll never loses anything: pin any past keyframe back as the start frame, free. Wiring any image into the card's socket overrides everything. Prefer to ground an invented shot on a real still after all? Pick one in its start selector; 🎨 generate in the same selector brings its keyframe back. That 🎨 entry is on every card: a grounded shot, or a shot you added yourself (+ in the board's header), switches to a generated keyframe too. Write its keyframe prompt (✏ on the card, the 🎨 line), check the anchor stills beside it (the still the card was on, by default; empty = every still on the board), 🎨. Until the prompt is written the card says so and the clip stays blocked downstream, never sent as text-to-video. Swap a start frame, generate a keyframe for an invented shot, drag a frame out to keep it **The film's aspect is your call.** The board's aspect dropdown (default: the plan's format) conforms every keyframe to the format you choose and stamps it into the emitted plan. Switching aspect later doesn't re-bill: the raw render is kept and simply re-cropped, free. Batch it. ▶ on the Storyboard (or the 🎨 Generate N button) renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation — shot list, per-frame price, total. The per-card 🎨 stays for surgical re-work. Declining isn't an error: the plan flows on and Film Shots simply blocks the frameless clips.
3 · The storyboard — your edit bay › End frames, on demand

A clip's end frame used to come only from your stills. Now every card's end selector offers three states: none, a still of the board, or 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right of the start frame — same image box, same in-socket and out-plug, same tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame (a still, a keyframe or a wired image), at the film's aspect. Where the camera arrives is now yours to direct, for grounded and invented shots alike. The prompt for that destination is drafted for you from the start frame, the shot's move and your reference board. Because a reveal or a pull-back shows what lies outside the start frame, the draft also picks the reference stills that show what the move reveals (at most three), so the destination comes from your real project, not from invention. It uses the planning model of the node feeding the plan wire: one text call, cents, in the ledger like the plan's. Nothing renders from a prompt you haven't seen: ✎ or 🎨 on the end block opens a review — the start frame beside the drafted prompt, editable in place, ✎ re-drafts, and the writer's still picks as toggleable thumbnails (tick more, untick any) — and Generate renders. Cancel keeps the text and renders nothing. ↻ re-rolls a rendered end frame, 📌 pins it (it then survives prompt edits and a re-rolled start frame — otherwise a new start honestly orphans its end, since the end continues it), 🕘 opens the card's end-frame history. Wiring any image into the end block's socket overrides everything, and the block's out-plug carries the resolved end frame wherever you want it. Every prompt a card owns has a plug, too, in a labeled plug bar at the card's bottom: prompt in / prompt out, 🎨 keyframe prompt on invented shots, ⇥ end prompt on armed cards — so any of them can feed a Refine or a Text Board, and you can read which is which. ▶ on the board covers end frames too: after the start keyframes, one review lists every armed card at once — drafts filled in, each editable — and one Generate renders them all. An armed end frame that isn't rendered yet blocks that clip in Film Shots, exactly like a missing start keyframe: it is never sent without it. And when the video model has no end-frame input (only some do — Kling 2.5+/3.0, Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0 among them), the clip still runs from its start frame, but the Film Shots table says so on that row — never silently. Budget-wise, an end frame is a second keyframe on that card (cents) plus one text call. Look at your frames. Click any card's image to magnify it full-screen, then browse the whole board like a gallery with ← / → (arrows or the on-screen ‹ ›); Esc closes. And every card has an output plug on its right edge carrying that clip's resolved start frame — the generated keyframe, the wired image, or the grounded still — so you can route a frame anywhere: into an Upscale Image for a delivery-res still, a Compose, a Preview. A card whose keyframe is still pending delivers nothing (never a wrong frame). The card's prompt has its own plug too, on the bottom-right — the final clip prompt, overrides and wired prompts applied — so a line of the DoP's wording can be reused or refined anywhere (a Refine, a Text Board, another card's prompt socket). And any card image can simply be dragged onto the canvas: it lands as a ready-filled Image In — detach a keyframe as the frozen base of a new exploration, safe from later re-plans.

Wire the Storyboard into Film Shots. It first adapts every clip prompt to the video model you picked (Kling, Seedance, Veo or Omni): a cheap text call per clip, done again only when you switch to another family; the table marks those rows ✦ and keeps the Director's text under them. It then prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, cost — and shows an itemized confirmation. Nothing generates until you approve the total; cancel a line and it updates. A tick box per row chooses what gets sent (untick = kept in the table, greyed, not sent — render a few, judge, then the rest). Cached and pinned clips cost $0. Then it fans out, staggered to respect rate limits, with per-clip re-roll / ✓✗ / pin. Every clip priced in the table, one itemized confirmation, nothing spends before your OK ## 5 · Review & cut The Clip Board plays every clip — keep the good, ✗ the misses, ↻ re-roll one. Route the keepers into a Sequence node, which assembles them into one mp4 with local ffmpeg — cuts or crossfades, clip audio kept, vertical reels stay vertical, free. Drop a Preview on the end. Two clips cut together with a crossfade and played in Preview: local ffmpeg on your machine, no cost Want it in 4K? Route a hero clip (or the assembled film) through **[Upscale Video](/docs/nodes/upscale.html)** — Topaz Proteus or Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend. The shipped **Finish in 4K** card is this stage on its own (one Upscale Video, target and upscaler on the face, provider unset: the money choice stays yours); it is the next card the Stills → Film card and the clip workflows offer once they hold a result.

The Stills → Film card is the reusable starting point, and any tuned chain of yours (a Director with your house style and dials, a Storyboard with your keyframe model) can be selected and collapsed into a composite or saved as your own template: one library item, every film starts warm. Why it holds together: every clip starts from a frame you have seen (a still of yours, or a keyframe generated from your stills), a shot without its frame never rolls, and every clip asks for a steady camera. The plan you approve is the film you get.
How do I resize a node?

Hover it: a small ⌟ grip fades in at the node's bottom-right corner (the same mark a text box has, applied to the whole node). Drag it to set width and height together; it lights up while you drag and fades out when you leave. Every resizable node uses this one gesture, boards, Preview, the text nodes, stickies and stamps alike, and the size is saved with the graph. Nothing to select first, and no frame around the node.
How do I send one output to several nodes?

Either drag a second wire from the same output port (an output can feed any number of inputs), or split an existing wire where you are: Alt-click the wire and a small dot drops on it. Drag a new wire off the dot to another node, or onto empty canvas to pick one from the add menu, already wired. The dot is only a branch point: nothing re-runs or re-pays because of it, and deleting it heals the wire. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I move all the wires from one pin to another?

Alt-click the pin whose wires you want to move (every pin starts pulsing), then click the destination pin. Output to output (or input to input) moves every wire across and keeps their other ends; an input then an output makes that output feed the input instead. Esc cancels, Ctrl+Z undoes. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I turn the home screen off?

Untick Show this screen at launch at the bottom of the home screen. Brut then opens straight on the canvas; the house icon on the left rail (above Settings) and File ▾ → Home still open it whenever you want it. The choice is per machine.
Why does a graph card show results I don't see on the canvas?

The card shows what the graph's saved file (or its live canvas, when it has unsaved changes) holds: the most recent results of its most downstream nodes, up to five. Hover the cover to flip through them. If a node's result was never saved with the graph (a run that finished after the last Ctrl+S), the card shows the canvas' own results and marks the name with a •.

Yes. Brut ships a bank of pre-wired workflows for the recurring jobs: Clay → Photoreal, Clay to Client Set, Time of Day, Weather & Sky, Populate, Populate → Clip, Scene Dressing, Editorial Sheet, Look Transfer, Hero Still → Clip, the Character Lab, Stills → Film, Reel Script and Finish in 4K, plus the Correction Loop template. They sit on the Workflows row of the home screen and on the From Brut shelf of the library (the book icon on the rail). Everything adds to your canvas: a composite as one card with knobs, a template as a group of live nodes. The full list, with what each one pins and what it takes in, is on the Workflows page.
Why does Marcel say there is nothing to recap?

Because nothing happened. At Narrator level Marcel recaps a project by himself the moment it opens, and the recap lands in his panel (the badge on the rail's Marcel button counts what you haven't read). A second recap is only worth a call when the diary holds at least five events and something new (a run, an error, a planner thought) happened since the last one; otherwise the engine skips the call and says so. Run something, then open the panel again.

During the beta, yes. At launch, Brut itself will be a paid tool: we sell the orchestration (the canvas, the caching that never re-bills unchanged work, the ledgers, the catalog kept current as providers churn, Marcel), never the tokens. Expect tiers with different feature sets, probably a limited free tier to see how it looks and a short trial; the exact terms are announced before launch. What never changes: generation is paid to the providers directly, on your own keys, at their price. Brut takes no cut, ever.
Where do my API keys go?

Into your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). They're used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider, are never written into a graph, never sent to us, and never appear in a .brutpack.
Can I cap what a project spends?

Yes — File ▾ → Project budget… sets a per-project ceiling compared against the ledger. The toolbar readout shows $spent / $budget and changes color as you approach it; paid confirmations warn past the cap (or refuse, if you tick hard cap). It's a guardrail on estimates, not accounting — the ledger stays the source of truth.
Can I turn a key off without deleting it?

Yes — every configured provider in ⚙ Settings has an on/off switch. Off = the saved key (or CLI sign-in) is ignored everywhere: the provider reads as unconfigured, and models with aggregator routes fall back to them — so you can test an OpenRouter-only setup, or bench a native key, without re-pasting anything. One tick brings it back.
Does Brut see my prompts, images or renders?

No. Everything you make stays on your disk (or your NAS). Brut has no server in the generation path. The only thing that ever leaves your machine is a tiny sign-in heartbeat — version/OS/install-id, no content.
Why do I have to sign in?

Today, to count seats during the beta. At launch, your account is also how you'll activate your plan on a machine. It's required, but it never bricks you: once you've signed in, a 30-day offline grace keeps you working through flights and outages, and if the sign-in server is unreachable a "continue for now" option appears. One exception, by design: a seat revoked for a breach of the beta license (a shared installer, a resold seat) signs out on that machine and paid generations stop until an active seat signs in. Nothing on disk is touched — your projects, outputs and keys stay yours.
Can I share Brut with a colleague?

Not the installer, please. Every beta seat is personal — that's the one rule of the beta license you accept in the app. Ask them to register on getbrut.app; applications are reviewed and approved seats get their own download link.
Windows says "Windows protected your PC" when I run the installer.

Expected during the beta: the installer isn't code-signed yet (a paid certificate we'll buy when the beta proves out), so SmartScreen flags it as unrecognized. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer runs per-user, without admin rights.
Where is my work on disk?

Everything Brut makes — projects, outputs, library, account state — lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut as plain files (keys are the exception: OS keychain). The engine's log is at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs\engine.log. Uninstalling never touches this folder — your work survives uninstall and reinstall. Text is ordinary text everywhere: select it and Ctrl+C copies it, in Marcel's messages, a node's result, a prompt. When nodes are selected on the canvas, Ctrl+C copies those nodes instead, unless you have text selected, in which case the text wins. Right-clicking selected text or a field offers the usual Copy, Cut, Paste and Select all. For any single image or video, right-click its preview. The same menu appears on every picture Brut shows, outputs and imports alike, board tiles, the magnifier, history rows: Send to chat attaches the image to your next message to Marcel (stills only), Decompose into layers… splits a picture into a base and up to 16 layers on Seedream 5.0 and lands them as a new Sketchpad (the one paid item of the menu: the price is shown first, and it is greyed with the reason without a BytePlus key), Reveal in Explorer opens the containing folder with the file selected (folders with spaces in their names included), Find in ledger shows the run that made the file (model, node, graph, prompt, parameters, cost, date) and can open that node's 🕘 history on the row, Copy file path copies where it lives, Copy image puts the pixels on the clipboard (a video gives its poster frame) to paste straight into Photoshop, a chat or a mail, Export JPG writes a full-resolution JPG (quality 92) and Export web JPG a 2048-pixel one (quality 85) into the project's outputs/exports folder, no dialog, and Explorer shows the file. A Sketchpad's preview also offers Export PSD (see the Sketchpad page). The right-click on an image never opens the ring menu: that is for empty canvas only. Reveal is the reliable way to locate a result, because outputs are written to whichever project was active when the generation ran. File ▾ → Save project as… later moves the files the canvas uses into the new project (with their history rows), so the new folder is complete; a file another graph in the old project also uses stays there as a copy, and anything you generated there that the canvas no longer references stays where it was.
What do the file names mean?

Every file Brut writes is named <project>_<graph>_<node>_<provider>_<model>_<date>_<job> — for example tournesol_facade-study_t2i-12_openai_GI25F_260923_a3f91c2e.png: the project, the graph, Text → Image node 12, made by OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Flare, on 23 Sept 2026, ledger job a3f91c2e…. The model codes (NB2, NBP, GI2, K30, SD25 …) are listed on the Projects page. Per-tile files say which tile (ms-4-s07, film-3-c02), files you drop in keep your own filename, and the free local tools name themselves (conform, layers, sketch, sequence). The last segment is the key: right-click → Find in ledger turns any file back into the run that made it. Files from before keep their old random names — renaming would break every cache and pin that references them. The full key, and how to set your own pattern per project, is on the Projects & the ledger page.

Grab the latest installer from getbrut.app/download (log in with your beta email — the page always serves the newest build) and run it over the old install — no uninstall needed. Projects, keys and sign-in all carry over (see the previous answer for why). There's no auto-update during the beta. You won't miss one, though: at every launch Brut compares the version you run with the latest installer (it rides the signed-in heartbeat, see Privacy). If yours is behind, one line under the toolbar says Brut x.y.z is available with a Download button to that page; Later hides it for that version. Same version, no line at all. Offline, no line either. To check which version you're on: File ▾ → About Brut, at the bottom of the menu.
The download page says the sign-in link "is invalid or has expired".

Something opened the link before you did. Company mail systems (Microsoft 365's Safe Links, Mimecast and the like) fetch every link in an incoming email to scan it, and a sign-in link works once, so the scan used it up and your click came second. The timing gives it away: the link is valid for an hour, yet the message appears right after the email arrives. Since October 2026 the emailed link lands on the download page and signs you in only when you press Continue there, so a scanner cannot spend it. The same email also carries an 8-digit code: type it on the download page instead, from any browser, if a link ever misbehaves. Links and codes work once and expire after an hour, so request a fresh email if yours is older than that. The desktop app's own sign-in screen takes the same code (builds from October 2026): after Email me a link, type the 8 digits from the email into the field that appears, no link needed.
The taskbar shows a blank document icon for Brut.

A bug in the installers from 1.0.95 to the first 1.1.2 builds: the shortcut they wrote carried a comment longer than Windows can read back, and the icon path stored after it came out garbled. The taskbar draws the icon of that shortcut, so it showed a blank page while the app itself was fine. Fixed in the 1.1.2 build re-uploaded on 2026-09-14: install it over your current one, it rewrites the Start Menu and desktop shortcuts and the window now declares its own icon. If you had pinned Brut to the taskbar before the fix, unpin it and pin it again once, the old pin kept a copy of the broken shortcut.
My first generation returned a 429. Why?

Almost always billing isn't enabled on that provider's key — free tiers have zero generation quota, so the first call fails. Enable billing in the provider's console. A first-call 429 is billing, not throttling.
An image edit came back blank / refused.

On Gemini, finishReason: OTHER (newer builds spell it IMAGE_OTHER) is a silent content refusal, usually triggered by an input image — a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo — not the prompt. Remove or crop the offending image. Brut never auto-retries it (it's deterministic).
Do I ever pay twice for the same thing?
No. Every node hashes its inputs; unchanged work is served from cache for $0. See Never pay twice.
What does ▶ Run do exactly? Does it generate everything?

No. ▶ Run is reveal-then-ask. Pass one replays every cached, pinned and free step for $0 and marks the nodes whose inputs changed (or that never ran) with a needs a run badge, together with what they would bill. If nothing needs a run, that's it. Otherwise one dialog lists them with the estimate: Generate runs the graph (cached steps still replay free; Film Shots, Upscale Video and the Storyboard keyframes still show their own itemized confirm first), Keep cached only leaves the badges on so you can see which nodes are outdated. The ▶ on a node runs that node and its upstream directly.
I reopened a graph and some results are missing.

Every generation node now shows its last result the moment the graph opens; the badge says whether it is current. If a node face is empty, it never produced a result in this graph. Hit ▶ Run to replay the cache and see what, if anything, would need generating.
I changed the prompt and lost a result I liked. Is it gone?

No — nothing generated is ever discarded. Every paid node has a small 🕘 in its title bar, next to ▶: it opens that node's full history from the project ledger, every result it ever produced. Pin any of them and it becomes the node's output again, free, protected from later re-runs until you unpin (the button turns 📌). Multi-Shot tiles, Storyboard keyframes and Film Shots clips have the same 🕘 per tile. See Projects & the ledger.
How do I take an image out of a node to work on it separately?

Drag it. Grab the image on any node — a generation preview, a Multi-Shot or Shot Board tile, a Reference Board still, a Storyboard card frame — and drop it on empty canvas: a ready-filled Image In appears there, pointing at the same file (no re-upload). Drop it on an existing Image In to append instead. The detached copy is a frozen base: re-rolling or re-planning the source never touches it.
A shot failed with "Network error — connection dropped mid-request".

Your connection to the provider dropped while a request was in flight (Wi-Fi blip, VPN hop, a provider hiccup). Re-roll the failed items — cached siblings won't re-pay. One honest caveat, written in the message itself: a response lost mid-read may still have generated (and billed) on the provider side; check the provider's console if it matters.
Can two people share a project?

Yes — put the project on a NAS and each seat opens the same folder, or pass a .brutpack file (warm caches included). There's no cloud sync by design; collaboration is file/NAS exchange. On a shared NAS project the studio timeline is shared too — one diary everyone writes to, with each entry tagged by who was signed in.

Two ways today. Export the project that holds it as a .brutpack (File ▾ → Export as pack): the graph travels with its outputs and warm caches, and the other seat opens it as a project. Or hand over the item itself: every saved composite or template is one JSON file in the library folder beside your projects (library/composites/<name>.json, library/templates/<name>.json); copy it into the same folder on the other machine and it appears on their Yours shelf. Library items hold recipes only, prompts, models and wiring, never images or keys, so they are safe to pass around. A shared community shelf is planned for later.

The Marcel button opens your project's studio timeline — a chronological record of runs, results, planner reasoning and errors, saved with the project so it survives restarts and travels with a NAS share — and the chat with Marcel, Brut's built-in companion. He knows the whole model catalog (with real prices), every node, and these docs; he answers on your own text-model key and every call lands in your spend ledger. An Assist slider sets how present he is on his own — from Off (silent journal) through failure diagnosis and run commentary up to Partner-level 💡 suggestions. A header toggle switches between the full engineer view and a chat-only view. It all stays on your machine (see Marcel, the companion and Privacy).
What happens if I kill the engine mid-render?
Video jobs are journaled and reattached on the next engine launch — same job ids, one ledger row, correct price. Paid work survives restarts.
Will I lose my canvas if I close the app?

No — the canvas autosaves into the project folder moments after every change, along with which named graph it is. Relaunch (any mode, any machine on a NAS share) and you're back exactly where you were. A • next to the graph name means changes not yet saved to the named graph (Ctrl+S), and opening another graph over unsaved work asks first.
Which video provider should I use?

For steady Kling use, the subscription is ~3× cheaper than API packs. Veo and Gemini Omni ride your Gemini key; Omni is the fast lane (a 10-second clip with sound in under a minute, flat ≈$1 per clip whatever the length — so ask for 10 s). Seedance 2.5 does native audio and single takes up to 30 seconds. All quote the cost before you spend.
How do I pay BytePlus for Seedance and Seedream?

One ModelArk key covers both, and billing is pay-as-you-go: top up Credits by card in the console (minimum USD 5, they never expire, USD 30 unlocks the Seedance family), or run Automatic billing on a bound card. Resource packs are optional (one model, 90 days, list price), and activating a model is a one-time switch on the console's Model activation page, needed before the first call. PayPal-only accounts need a card or a pack. Details on the Seedance page; Seedream 5.0 Lite comes with 50 free images.
What does "⇄ runs via …" on a node mean?

You picked a model whose native provider has no key on this machine, but you hold a credential for an aggregator that resells the same model — so Brut routes the run there, on your account. Your direct key always wins when present (it's usually cheaper); routing only fills the gap, it's always shown on the node and in the run confirm, and the ledger records it. Brut is built local-first, and privacy isn't a policy bolted on afterward — it's the architecture. Here is, precisely, what stays on your machine and what (very little) leaves it.

Your prompts, images, renders and video. All of it is written to your disk (or your NAS), inside your project's outputs/ folder. Brut has no server in the generation path — your work is never uploaded to us, and we cannot see it. Your graphs and projects. Stored locally as files. A .brutpack or NAS share moves them between your machines; nothing routes through a cloud. Your API keys. Stored in your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). Used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider. Never written into a graph, never sent to us, never in a .brutpack. The engine log. The desktop app writes the engine's console output to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs so problems can be diagnosed. It stays on your disk — a feedback report never includes it unless you attach it yourself. And the app never phones home for updates: the beta has no auto-update, so there's no update check leaving your machine either. Generation calls go from your machine straight to the provider (Google, OpenAI, Kling, Magnific, Topaz, …) on your key. Those providers see the requests you send them, under their own privacy terms — Brut is never in the middle. One provider-side detail worth knowing: Gemini Omni runs on Google's Interactions API, which keeps each interaction (prompt, input images, the generated clip) on Google's side for a while after it completes — that is the mechanism that lets the model edit its own earlier clips. Same key, same Google terms as Gemini and Veo. To be precise about that promise: there is no aggregator that Brut operates in the call path — no server of ours, ever. If you choose to run a model through a route (an aggregator you subscribe to yourself, when you hold no direct key), your requests go from your machine straight to that service, on your credential, under its privacy terms — and the node, the confirm dialog and the ledger always say so. One provider sends nothing at all: video upscales through Topaz Video AI (local) run entirely on your own GPU via the Topaz desktop app you installed — the clip never leaves your machine. One setup step downloads a tool rather than talking to a provider: clicking Install Kling CLI (for the Kling subscription provider) fetches Kling's official command-line client from the npm public registry — a one-time, user-initiated download of about 1 MB, integrity-checked, carrying no data of yours beyond the download request itself. Brut never auto-downloads anything.

Brut keeps a studio timeline per project — the running record of runs, results, and your conversations with Marcel, the built-in companion. It lives in a plain text file inside the project (ledger/activity.jsonl), on your disk or your NAS, and is never uploaded — it travels only where the project itself travels. When you export a project to a folder it's included by default (it's a backup); when you make a .brutpack to hand off, it's left out by default — a checkbox lets you decide either way each time. Chatting with Marcel works like every generation: the conversation goes from your machine straight to the text-model provider you picked (Google, OpenAI or Anthropic), on your own key, under that provider's terms. Brut is never in the middle, and every call is written to your local spend ledger with its token counts and cost. Images you attach to a chat message (the 📎 button, Send to chat, a pasted or dropped file, or the stills of a node you name in the message) are sent to that same provider as part of that one message — never re-sent on later turns, and only files inside your project's outputs can be attached at all (a file you paste or drop from elsewhere is imported into the project first, like any image you bring in). The composer tells you before sending when naming a node will attach its stills. When Marcel acts on your canvas, what he reads to do the job — your graph's structure, node prompts and parameters, output file names, journal search results — becomes part of that same conversation, so it reaches the text provider you picked, and nothing else. The actions themselves (placing nodes, wiring, running) happen entirely on your machine, and anything that would bill a key stops at an itemized confirm first. When Marcel speaks up on his own (the Assist slider at Reactive and above — failure diagnoses, run commentary, the recap when you open a project), the material he reasons over is the same local record: recent timeline lines, the error text, what's still running. That goes to your chosen text provider on your key, exactly like a chat message, and each remark is a ledgered call you can see. Set the slider to Off and nothing is ever sent unprompted. What Marcel remembers also stays on your disk. He keeps a taste profile — a plain-text note about how you like your images — tied to your account and stored beside your library. It is per-account, private, and never synced or exported: it does not travel in a folder export or a .brutpack. Project notes (a small memory for each project) live inside the project and travel with it, like the timeline. Both are plain text you can open and edit; Marcel proposes additions from your recent work and applies nothing to the profile until you approve it.
The local engine is locked to the app

Brut runs a small engine on your own machine (127.0.0.1). To make sure only the Brut app can drive it — and not some other web page you happen to have open in the same browser — the engine mints a secret token when it starts and requires it on every action that spends money or changes your files. The app receives that token automatically; nothing else on your machine can guess it, so nothing else can make Brut generate, delete, or spend on your behalf.
The only thing Brut ever sends

When you're signed in, the engine sends a small heartbeat — at startup and once a day — so we can count active seats during the beta. That's it. Here is the entire payload, verbatim: { "install_id": "a uuid minted once on this machine", "app_version": "…", "engine_version": "…", "os": "Windows", "os_version": "…", "arch": "…", "ts": "…", "eula_version": "the date of the beta license you accepted" } No content. No prompts, no images, no filenames, no graph data — ever. By construction: the code only ever assembles those eight fields. The license version you accepted. The date stamp of the beta license you clicked I accept on in the app — so we can show, if ever asked, that a seat took the terms. A date, nothing more. Nothing while signed out. If you're not signed in, no heartbeat is sent at all. The answer carries two things back: whether your beta seat is still active, and the version number of the latest installer. If a seat is revoked for a breach of the beta license, Brut signs you out and stops paid generations on that machine; your projects, outputs and keys stay exactly where they are. If the latest installer is newer than the one you run, a single line under the toolbar says so with a link to the download page; same version, no line. Nothing extra leaves your machine for that check: the version you run was already in the heartbeat. You can see this exact JSON any time in ⚙ Settings → Account.
Feedback — only what you type, only when you click send

The 💬 Send feedback button is the one other thing that can send data, and it's entirely user-initiated: nothing is ever sent until you press Send. A report carries your message, your account email (so we can reply), and — only if you leave the checkbox on — a diagnostics block: the same eight heartbeat fields plus the last few error messages from the Activity panel. The modal shows that block byte for byte before you send it ("Show exactly what will be sent"). Never your graphs, images, prompts or keys. The desktop app's quit-time prompt ("Before you go") is the same form under the same rule: it appears only after a session that actually ran something, and nothing leaves your machine unless you press Send & quit. Quit without sending is always one click.

Identity runs through Supabase (magic link or Google/GitHub). It's used only to know who's using a seat — never to store your work. The engine holds your session, not the browser: your refresh token is kept in your OS keychain, and access tokens are verified locally against a cached public key (so it works offline). This is identity only.

getbrut.app and this documentation load nothing from third parties — fonts are self-hosted, and there are no analytics scripts or trackers. The site has its own short notice covering the beta form, sign-in and emails: getbrut.app/privacy. The beta sign-up form is the one place you hand us an email, and only if you choose to. When your seat is approved we send one approval email to that address, and the download page asks you to sign in with the same Supabase account the app uses — that sign-in is checked against the approved list to serve the installer, and nothing else is recorded.

Your keys, your work, your machine. The only thing we ever learn is that a version of Brut is running on some install, on some OS — and only while you're signed in. Exports made from the right-click menu (JPG, web JPG, PSD) are local files written into the active project's outputs/exports folder. Nothing is uploaded or shared by that menu.
